title: Merkle's Boner
summary: Fred Merkle, nineteen and filling in for an injured regular, never touched second on what should have been the winning single. The league called it a tie, they played it over, and the Cubs took the pennant.
story:
September 23, 1908. The Polo Grounds.

Bottom of the ninth, two out, the Giants and Cubs tied for the game and tied for first. Fred Merkle, filling in for the injured Fred Tenney, stands on first. Moose McCormick is on third. Al Bridwell singles. McCormick trots home. The crowd spills onto the field, certain New York has won.

Merkle does what a lot of runners did when the winning run had already scored: he peels off toward the clubhouse without touching second.

Johnny Evers notices.

Which baseball eventually reaches Evers is still disputed. What is not disputed is that he steps on second, and that umpire Hank O'Day calls Merkle out. O'Day had seen a nearly identical play by the Pirates' Warren Gill on September 4 and let it pass. This time he does not. The field is too chaotic to finish the game. The league rules it a tie.

They play it over on October 8. Mordecai Brown beats Christy Mathewson, 4–2, and Chicago wins the pennant by that game.

Merkle went on to a long, respectable career and hated the word bonehead. The catalog keeps the name history gave the play, and records that he asked not to be remembered by it.
counterfactual: Merkle touches second. Bridwell's single stands, McCormick's run counts, and the Giants win it on September 23. There is no tie, no October 8 replay, and no 4–2 game for Brown to take from Mathewson. Chicago has to catch New York some other way, or it never does. Merkle is a nineteen-year-old who did his job on a game-winning hit, not a nickname.

images.credit: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

images.caption: Fred Merkle on a contemporary baseball card. This is a portrait, not a photograph of the play.
images.credit: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

damage.stakes: The Giants and Cubs were tied for first. The single would have won the game.

title: Snodgrass's Muff
summary: With the Giants one win from a title, Fred Snodgrass dropped a routine fly to open the tenth. In the same half-inning he made a fine catch the nickname forgot.
story:
October 16, 1912. Fenway Park.

The World Series has needed an eighth game because one of the first seven ended in a tie. Christy Mathewson carries a 2–1 lead into the bottom of the tenth. Clyde Engle leads off with a routine fly to center.

Fred Snodgrass drops it. Engle reaches second.

The inning does not belong to that drop alone. Snodgrass then runs down Harry Hooper's long drive and catches it. Steve Yerkes walks. Tris Speaker lifts a foul pop that Mathewson, first baseman Fred Merkle, and catcher Chief Meyers all hesitate on. It falls safely. Speaker singles Engle home. Larry Gardner's sacrifice fly scores Yerkes, and Boston wins, 3–2.

The error picked up the nickname the "$30,000 muff," a figure that overstated the actual gap between the winners' and losers' shares. Snodgrass spent the rest of his life attached to the drop. The catch on Hooper happened in the same half-inning.
counterfactual: Snodgrass squeezes the first fly. Engle is out, and the tenth starts the way a one-run lead is supposed to start. Speaker's foul, Yerkes's walk, Gardner's fly — those may still have arrived. Or Mathewson walks off with the title he carried into the inning. What does not arrive is the nickname. The catch on Hooper is just another play, not the one the retelling forgot.

images.caption: Fred Snodgrass of the New York Giants in 1911, the year before the dropped fly. The negative is labeled with his name.
images.credit: Public domain. Bain News Service, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons.

images.caption: Fred Snodgrass. The portrait predates the reputation the tenth inning gave him.
images.credit: Public domain. George Grantham Bain Collection, via Wikimedia Commons.

damage.stakes: The deciding game of the World Series had gone to the tenth. The inning was just starting.

title: Germany Schaefer Steals First
summary: With the game tied in the ninth, Germany Schaefer stole second, got nothing for it, and stole first base back. The rules eventually made the trick illegal.
story:
A story in Lawrence Ritter's The Glory of Their Times has Germany Schaefer stealing first against Cleveland in 1908, told years later by teammate Davy Jones. The details do not survive contact with the newspapers. Historians treat that version as folklore.

The documented one is August 4, 1911. Washington against the White Sox, the score tied in the bottom of the ninth.

Clyde Milan is on third. Schaefer is on first. He steals second, hoping catcher Fred Payne will throw and let Milan come home. Payne holds the ball.

On the next pitch Schaefer takes off back toward first.

Umpire Tommy Connolly lets it stand. There is no rule against running the bases in reverse. White Sox manager Hugh Duffy comes out to argue. While he does, Schaefer breaks for second again, is caught in a rundown, and Milan is thrown out trying to score.

Connolly said afterward that Schaefer had a perfect right to go from second back to first. In 1920, after Schaefer's death, the rules changed: a runner who reverses direction to confuse the defense, or to make a travesty of the game, is out.

The trick worked once, on paper. It did not score the run. It scored a paragraph in the rulebook instead.

title: Zimmerman Chases Collins Home
summary: In Game 6 of the 1917 World Series, nobody covered home plate, so Heinie Zimmerman ran Eddie Collins across it himself.
story:
October 15, 1917. The Polo Grounds.

The White Sox lead the World Series three games to two. In the fourth inning Eddie Collins is on third and Joe Jackson on first. Happy Felsch bounces back to pitcher Rube Benton.

Catcher Bill Rariden has come up the line to start a rundown. Neither Benton nor first baseman Walter Holke covers the plate.

Heinie Zimmerman, the third baseman, has the ball and an empty home plate in front of him. He chases Collins — one of the quickest men in the league — all the way across it.

The inning is already messy. Zimmerman has thrown a ball away, and right fielder Dave Robertson has dropped a fly. The footrace is what the papers keep. New York adds Zimmerman to the list of Giants scapegoats that already includes Fred Merkle and Fred Snodgrass.

John McGraw does not. He puts the blame on Benton and Holke for leaving the plate uncovered. Chicago wins the game, 4–2, and the series with it.

The picture is a third baseman running a man home. The failure was the empty plate he was running toward.
counterfactual: Benton covers the plate, or Holke does. Zimmerman throws home instead of giving chase, and Collins is tagged out in a rundown that looks like baseball. The fourth inning does not become a footrace. The White Sox might still have closed the Series that afternoon — they were the club that led it three games to two — but Zimmerman is not the man in the photograph, and the Giants' list of scapegoats stops a name shorter.

damage.stakes: Game 6 of the World Series, fourth inning. The catcher had left the plate, and nobody else covered it.

title: The Sale of Babe Ruth
summary: The Red Sox sold Babe Ruth to the Yankees for $100,000, paid in installments. The Broadway story that explains the sale is a myth.
story:
January 5, 1920. The announcement comes first, before any pitch of the new decade.

The Yankees have bought Babe Ruth from the Boston Red Sox. The price is $100,000, paid in installments of $25,000 at six percent interest. A separate loan of $300,000 from Yankees owner Jacob Ruppert to Red Sox owner Harry Frazee, secured by a mortgage on Fenway Park, follows that May. Ruppert holds the mortgage until Tom Yawkey retires it in 1933.

The story everyone knows is that Frazee sold Ruth to finance the musical No, No, Nanette. That show did not open until 1925. Frazee was a theater man, and he did need cash, but the sale also sat inside his feud with American League president Ban Johnson and a more complicated set of debts than one production. The Nanette explanation is a myth that stuck because it is tidy.

The consequences were not tidy. Ruth became the player who changed the sport. The Yankees won their first pennant in 1921. The Red Sox did not win another World Series until 2004.

Calling the sale a blunder is hindsight. On the day it was announced, it was also a choice: trade the best player in baseball for money and a mortgage.
counterfactual: Frazee keeps him. The home runs stay in Fenway, and the mortgage on the park is someone else's problem, or it is solved some other way. New York's first pennant, in 1921, arrives later, or arrives without Ruth at the center of it. Boston does not wait until 2004 to win another World Series. The Broadway myth never has a ballplayer to attach itself to.

images.caption: Babe Ruth in a Boston uniform in 1919, the season before the Yankees bought his contract. This is a publicity portrait, not a photograph of the sale.
images.credit: Public domain. National Photo Company, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons.

damage.stakes: Boston sold its best player for cash, paid in installments.

title: Peckinpaugh's Eight Errors
summary: The American League's Most Valuable Player committed eight errors in the 1925 World Series, two of them in a rainy seventh game the Senators had led.
story:
October 15, 1925. Forbes Field, in a downpour that turns the ball dark and the infield to mud.

Roger Peckinpaugh is not a clumsy shortstop having a moment. He is the American League's Most Valuable Player, and Washington had led this World Series three games to one. Pittsburgh has won two since. Now it is Game 7.

Walter Johnson takes a 6–4 lead into the seventh. Eddie Moore pops up — the sort of ball Peckinpaugh catches as a matter of course — and he drops it. His seventh error of the series. Max Carey scores. Pie Traynor triples to tie the game before being thrown out at home.

Peckinpaugh answers with a home run in the eighth to make it 7–6.

In the bottom of the inning he cannot handle Carey's grounder. His eighth error, still the World Series record. Kiki Cuyler's double puts the Pirates ahead.

Pittsburgh wins, 9–7, and becomes the first team to come back from a 3–1 deficit in a best-of-seven World Series. The rain was real. So was the record. So was the home run in between, which the retelling rarely bothers to keep.

title: Three Men on Third
summary: Babe Herman doubled off the right-field screen at Ebbets Field and arrived at third to find two teammates already there.
story:
August 15, 1926. Ebbets Field, the first game of a doubleheader.

Brooklyn has the bases loaded against the Braves in the seventh, with one out. Hank DeBerry is on third, pitcher Dazzy Vance on second, Chick Fewster on first. Babe Herman drives the ball off the right-field screen. Under the ground rules it is still in play. DeBerry scores.

Vance, not a practiced baserunner, holds up to see if the ball will be caught, then tries to score, is cut off, and retreats. He gets back to third at the same time Fewster and Herman arrive.

Third baseman Eddie Taylor tags all three.

Vance is the lead runner and is not forced, so he is entitled to the base. Fewster and Herman are out. Herman has doubled into a double play, and the run he drove in stands up as the winner.

He spent years pointing out that nobody remembered the run, only the crowd on the bag. The telling grew until people called it a triple play. It was not. There was already one out. It was strange enough without the embroidery.

title: Hack Wilson Loses the Ball in the Sun
summary: The Cubs led Game 4 of the 1929 World Series by eight runs. In the seventh, Hack Wilson lost a fly ball in the sun, and the Athletics scored ten.
story:
October 12, 1929. Shibe Park.

Game 4 looks finished early. The Cubs lead Connie Mack's Athletics, 8–0.

In the bottom of the seventh Philadelphia sends ten runs across — the largest inning in World Series history at the time — and wins the game, 10–8.

The play in the middle of it is Mule Haas's fly to center. Hack Wilson loses the ball in the sun. It falls behind him and becomes a three-run inside-the-park home run, and the inning keeps going.

Wilson was not a poor player having a poor series so much as a great hitter — he would set the National League record with 191 runs batted in the next season — who had one terrible moment in the outfield with the title in reach.

The Athletics close out the series the next day. Wilson's name stays attached to the sun.
counterfactual: Wilson finds the ball. Haas is out, and an eight-run lead in the seventh is usually enough to finish the afternoon. The Athletics might still have come back some other way, or they might have closed the series the next day anyway. What does not happen is a three-run inside-the-park homer that nobody saw come down, or a man's name hung on the sun.

damage.stakes: Game 4 of the World Series. Chicago led by eight runs in the seventh.

title: Medwick and the Fruit Barrage
summary: After a hard slide in Game 7, Detroit fans threw fruit, bottles, and vegetables at Joe Medwick until the commissioner took him out of the game.
story:
October 9, 1934. Navin Field, Game 7.

The Cardinals are already blowing out the Tigers when Joe Medwick slides hard into third baseman Marv Owen. Detroit does not appreciate it.

When Medwick goes back to left field, the crowd pelts him with fruit, bottles, and vegetables. Play stops.

Commissioner Kenesaw Mountain Landis is in the ballpark. He removes Medwick from the game — not as a punishment entered in a box score, but because the left fielder is no longer safe. St. Louis wins, 11–0, and the Gashouse Gang has its championship.

Medwick's bat is not the story of the afternoon by then. The crowd is.

It is an early, unmistakable case of a ballpark deciding it would rather throw things than watch the rest of a lost game. The commissioner sided with getting his player off the field.

title: Owen's Dropped Third Strike
summary: The Dodgers were one strike from tying the World Series. Mickey Owen missed the third strike, and the Yankees scored four runs.
story:
October 5, 1941. Ebbets Field, Game 4 of the World Series.

Brooklyn leads 4–3 with two out in the ninth. Hugh Casey is pitching to Tommy Henrich. Henrich swings and misses.

The inning, and a tied series, appear to be over.

The ball gets past catcher Mickey Owen, all the way to the screen, and Henrich reaches first. Whether Casey's breaking ball was doctored is still argued and is not required to explain the rest.

Joe DiMaggio singles. Charlie Keller doubles. Bill Dickey walks. Joe Gordon doubles. The Yankees score four and win, 7–4. They take the series the next day.

Owen was an All-Star catcher, not a cartoon. One missed pitch with two out in October rewrote the game, and then the retelling rewrote Owen. The four hits that followed the miss are part of the inning too.
counterfactual: The ball stays in the mitt. Henrich is out. Brooklyn wins, 4–3, and the Series is even heading into Game 5. The Yankees might still have taken it the next day, or the day after that. What does not happen is four New York hits after a swing-and-miss that should have ended the night. Owen remains an All-Star who caught the last strike, not the man the retelling rewrote.

images.caption: Mickey Owen in 1942. This is not the passed ball in the 1941 World Series.
images.credit: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

damage.stakes: One strike from a win that would have tied the World Series.

title: Eddie Gaedel Walks
summary: Bill Veeck sent 3-foot-7 Eddie Gaedel to the plate in a child's uniform. Gaedel walked on four pitches. The league voided the contract the next day.
story:
August 19, 1951. Sportsman's Park, the second game of a doubleheader, Browns against the Tigers.

Between games, a cake is wheeled out for the fiftieth anniversary of the American League. Out of it, in Browns owner Bill Veeck's telling of the stunt, comes Eddie Gaedel, 3 feet 7 inches, wearing number 1/8.

Manager Zack Taylor sends him up to bat for Frank Saucier, a legitimate contract in hand. Bob Cain walks him on four pitches. Gaedel never takes the bat off his shoulder. Jim Delsing runs for him.

The next day American League president Will Harridge voids the contract and tells clubs not to try it again. Gaedel's entire major-league career is one walk.

The joke, such as it was, belonged to Veeck. Gaedel was a performer who had been hired, paid, and let in on the stunt. He remains the shortest player in major-league history. The catalog keeps the entry for the promotion, not as a joke at his expense.

images.caption: Eddie Gaedel, 3-foot-7, in his batting stance for the St. Louis Browns as Detroit catcher Bob Swift kneels, August 19, 1951.
images.credit: Associated Press, ACME Newspictures or team photographer, via The Philadelphia Inquirer, August 20, 1951. Public domain (PD-US-not renewed).

damage.stakes: The second game of a doubleheader. He walked on four pitches and never took the bat off his shoulder.

title: The Shot Heard 'Round the World
summary: Bobby Thomson's pennant-winning homer off Ralph Branca is one of the famous swings in the sport. The Giants had stolen the sign.
story:
October 3, 1951. The Polo Grounds, the third and final game of a National League playoff.

The Dodgers lead 4–1 going into the ninth. Alvin Dark and Don Mueller single. Whitey Lockman doubles. It is 4–2, runners on second and third. Mueller hurts himself sliding and is replaced by a pinch runner. Don Newcombe comes out. Ralph Branca comes in.

Thomson hits a three-run homer. The Giants win, 5–4.

Russ Hodges's call entered the language:

> The Giants win the pennant! The Giants win the pennant!

For decades that was the whole story. Later research, especially Joshua Prager's, and the accounts of the participants, established that the Giants had been stealing signs with a telescope in the clubhouse beyond center field. Herman Franks relayed them to the bullpen, and the bullpen relayed them to the hitter. Thomson later said he knew what was coming.

The homer was real. The information was stolen. Branca spent a life as the man who threw the pitch. He also spent it as the man who was pitched against with a telescope in the building behind him. Both facts belong in the record.
counterfactual: There is no telescope in the clubhouse beyond center field. Thomson still might have hit it — he was a real hitter taking a real swing — but he would have been guessing with everyone else. Branca would have been beaten by a pitch, not by a building. The call would still have entered the language. The later knowledge that Thomson knew would not.

damage.stakes: The deciding playoff game, bottom of the ninth, with the Giants down by two.

title: Throneberry Misses the Base
summary: Marv Throneberry hit what looked like a two-run triple and was called out for missing first. He later admitted he had missed second, too.
story:
June 17, 1962. The Polo Grounds, the first game of a doubleheader against the Cubs.

The Mets of 1962 will lose 120 games, and Marvelous Marv Throneberry will become their emblem. The clearest single play arrives in the first inning, with New York trailing 4–1. Throneberry drives a ball into the right-center gap. Two runs score. He pulls into third.

Ernie Banks appeals. Umpire Dusty Boggess calls Throneberry out for missing first base.

The story that Casey Stengel came out to argue, and was told not to bother because Throneberry had missed second as well, has been told as an umpire's quip. The better-sourced version is that first-base coach Cookie Lavagetto was the one who stopped Stengel. The next day's New York Times mentioned only the miss at first. Retrosheet notes that Throneberry admitted he had missed second, too.

The Cubs win, 8–7. Throneberry strikes out in the ninth with the tying run on base. The legend grew a few extra punch lines. The missed base did not need them.

title: Brock for Broglio
summary: The Cubs traded Lou Brock to the Cardinals for Ernie Broglio in a six-player deal. Brock finished with 3,023 hits. Broglio won seven games in Chicago.
story:
June 15, 1964. A six-player deal hits the transaction wire, and on that day it has a logic.

The Cubs send Lou Brock, Jack Spring, and Paul Toth to St. Louis for Ernie Broglio, Bobby Shantz, and Doug Clemens. Broglio is 28 and has won 18 games the year before. Brock is a young outfielder hitting .251, striking out too often for a man at the top of a lineup.

It does not survive the summer. Brock hits .348 the rest of the way, and the Cardinals win the pennant and the World Series. Broglio goes 7–19 as a Cub and is out of the majors after 1966. He later said his elbow was already damaged when the trade was made, and that he had been taking cortisone. Brock retired with 3,023 hits and 938 stolen bases.

The trade is the shorthand for a deal that cannot be walked back. It is also a reminder that the famous side of it was not obvious in the transaction wire. Broglio was the established pitcher. The elbow was the fact the Cubs did not price in.
counterfactual: Chicago keeps Brock. The Cardinals find another outfielder; they might still have won that autumn, or they might not. What does not happen is 3,023 hits and 938 stolen bases in another team's colors. Broglio's elbow is still Broglio's elbow. The Cubs, for once, are the club that waited to see what the young outfielder would become.

damage.stakes: A six-player deal in June. The player who left had his career in front of him.

title: The Phillies' 1964 Collapse
summary: Philadelphia led the league by 6½ games with twelve to play. Gene Mauch kept running his aces out on short rest. The Phillies lost ten in a row.
story:
September 21, 1964. Morning in Philadelphia: the Phillies are 90–60 and lead the National League by 6½ games, with twelve left.

That night, at home against Cincinnati, Chico Ruiz steals home in the sixth with Frank Robinson at the plate. Art Mahaffey's pitch gets away. Ruiz scores. The Reds win, 1–0.

Manager Gene Mauch cannot believe anyone would steal home with Robinson batting. Ruiz is safe. The steal works.

What follows is the managerial entry. The Phillies lose ten in a row. Mauch keeps sending Jim Bunning and Chris Short back to the mound on short rest, sometimes on two days. Over the final twelve games Philadelphia goes 2–10. The Cardinals go 9–3 and win the pennant on the last afternoon. The Phillies win their finale, 10–0, which is no longer relevant.

Ruiz's dash is the folk beginning of the slide. The repeated decision to empty the two best arms is the part a manager could control.

title: Frank Robinson for Milt Pappas
summary: Cincinnati's Bill DeWitt called Frank Robinson an old thirty and traded him to Baltimore. The next year Robinson won the Triple Crown.
story:
December 9, 1965. The Reds trade Frank Robinson to the Orioles for Milt Pappas, Jack Baldschun, and Dick Simpson.

Robinson is thirty. Owner Bill DeWitt, explaining the deal, calls him an old thirty. The phrase is the part that lasted, because the next season made it look absurd.

In 1966 Robinson hits .316 with 49 home runs and 122 runs batted in, wins the Triple Crown and the American League Most Valuable Player award, and is the World Series MVP when Baltimore sweeps the Dodgers. He plays six seasons in Baltimore, makes four World Series, and wins two of them. Pappas is a capable pitcher who is not Frank Robinson. Baldschun and Simpson do not change that.

DeWitt wanted pitching, and thirty is not young for a corner outfielder of that era. The record does not require pretending the Reds received nothing. It does require noticing that they gave away a player who was not finished.
counterfactual: DeWitt keeps him. The next season's numbers belong to Cincinnati, not to a man another club was told was already old. Baltimore still has a good team; it does not have the hitter who swept the Dodgers as World Series MVP. "An old thirty" is never said, or is said about someone else.

damage.stakes: A thirty-year-old outfielder, traded for pitching. The next season he won the Triple Crown.

title: Nolan Ryan for Jim Fregosi
summary: The Mets traded Nolan Ryan and three others to the Angels for Jim Fregosi. Ryan left with seven no-hitters. Fregosi was gone in a season and a half.
story:
December 10, 1971. The Mets send Nolan Ryan, Leroy Stanton, Don Rose, and Francisco Estrada to the California Angels for shortstop Jim Fregosi.

Ryan is 24, wild, and unfinished: a hard thrower the Mets have not found a consistent role for. Fregosi is a six-time All-Star. The Mets think they are buying a shortstop and selling a project.

Ryan wins 324 games, strikes out 5,714 batters, and throws seven no-hitters. Fregosi's 101 games in 1972 are the last season he reaches 100. The Mets move him on after a year and a half. He later manages the 1993 Phillies to the World Series, which is a better ending than the trade-wire version of him as a punch line.

The deal is still the cleanest example of a franchise giving up on a pitcher one organization too soon. The Angels did not invent Ryan. They waited him out.
counterfactual: The Mets wait. The no-hitters, if they come, come in New York, and a franchise that already had Seaver has Ryan too. Fregosi is someone else's shortstop. Or the wildness never settles, and the patience looks foolish in the other direction. What the Angels proved is that someone had to wait. The Mets chose not to be that club.

damage.stakes: A young pitcher traded for a veteran infielder the club wanted sooner.

title: Ten-Cent Beer Night
summary: Cleveland sold beer for a dime, the limit collapsed, and the crowd stormed the field. The umpires forfeited the game to Texas.
story:
June 4, 1974. Cleveland Stadium.

The Indians, trying to fill a ballpark that is usually empty, price beer at ten cents. Other clubs have tried the same promotion with a hard limit of two. Cleveland's limit of six is not enforced once the concession stands fall behind, and fans are allowed to fill cups from Stroh's trucks parked behind the outfield fence. The crowd is 25,134, more than double the usual draw.

The night has a grudge in it. A week earlier there was trouble in Texas, and Rangers manager Billy Martin joked that Cleveland did not have enough fans to worry about.

People run onto the field through the game. In the ninth a fan goes after right fielder Jeff Burroughs's cap. Martin leads his players out, some of them carrying bats. The Indians come out to help the visitors. Reliever Tom Hilgendorf is hit with a chair.

Crew chief Nestor Chylak, injured in the melee, forfeits the game to Texas, 9–0. The promotion had worked. The ballgame had not survived it.
counterfactual: The six-beer cap holds. The trucks stay closed. The ninth is played, and somebody wins it without a forfeit, without a chair, and without the visitors needing an escort. Martin's joke stays a joke. Chylak goes home unhurt. Cleveland still has a promotion that filled the park. It also has a game that finished.

images.caption: Rangers' Mike Hargrove punches a fan held down by teammate Alex Johnson during Ten-Cent Beer Night at Cleveland Stadium, June 4, 1974.
images.credit: Paul Tepley / The Cleveland Press. Public domain (PD-US-no notice), via Wikimedia Commons.

damage.stakes: Beer was a dime, and the limit was not kept. The umpires forfeited the game in the ninth.

title: Herb Washington Is Picked Off
summary: Charlie Finley signed a world-class sprinter who had never played baseball and used him only as a pinch runner. In the World Series, Mike Marshall picked him off.
story:
October 13, 1974. Dodger Stadium, Game 2 of the World Series.

Herb Washington is a sprinter, a Michigan State man who held world-class times and had no baseball career behind him. Charlie Finley signed him in 1974 as a designated runner. He appeared in 92 games that year, stole 29 bases, and never came to the plate. His career, ended when the A's released him in May 1975, was 105 games, 31 steals, 17 times caught stealing, and no at-bats.

The World Series exposes the experiment in one pitch. Oakland has just scored twice and trails 3–2 in the ninth. Washington runs for Joe Rudi, the tying run, at first base.

Mike Marshall — the Dodgers' relief pitcher, and another former Spartan — picks him off. Steve Garvey puts the tag on. Marshall then strikes out the next hitter. The A's lose the game and win the series anyway.

Washington was asked to do one thing he had never practiced under major-league pickoff moves. Finley was the one who sent him out there to learn it in October.

title: Disco Demolition Night
summary: The White Sox blew up a crate of disco records between games of a doubleheader. Fans took the field, a fire started, and the second game was forfeited.
story:
July 12, 1979. Comiskey Park, a twi-night doubleheader between the White Sox and the Tigers.

Mike Veeck, Bill Veeck's son, and WLUP disc jockeys Steve Dahl and Garry Meier have built a promotion around the backlash against disco: 98 cents to get in if you brought a record to destroy. Between games, a crate of records is blown up in center field.

Thousands of people have come, many of them not there for baseball. After the explosion the crowd storms the field. A fire burns. The grass is ruined. The umpires forfeit the second game to Detroit.

What had been planned as a gag between games of a doubleheader ends with one of those games never being played.

The night is also part of a wider reaction against disco that overlapped with hostility toward Black and gay culture. Remembering it only as a funny forfeit leaves that out. Remembering it only as a culture-war parable leaves out the simpler operational fact: the club invited a crowd it could not control, and then lost the field.
counterfactual: The crate is a photo opportunity, and the crowd stays in the seats. The second game is played. Detroit or Chicago wins it on the field, and the grass survives the night. The promotion is still a gag about records. It is not a forfeit, and it is not a fire.

images.caption: Thousands of fans storm the field at Comiskey Park during the disco record-burning stunt, July 12, 1979, forcing the second game to be forfeited.
images.credit: Fred Jewell. Public domain (PD-US-1978-89), via Wikimedia Commons.

videos.title: Remembering Disco Demolition Night
videos.description: An MLB Network look back at the July 12, 1979 promotion. This is not footage of the forfeit itself.

damage.stakes: The second game of a doubleheader had not been played. The crowd was on the field.

title: The Pine Tar Game
summary: George Brett's go-ahead homer was taken off the board because there was too much pine tar on the bat. The league president put the homer back.
story:
July 24, 1983. Yankee Stadium.

George Brett hits a two-run homer off Goose Gossage in the ninth, and Kansas City takes the lead. Billy Martin asks the umpires to look at the bat. The rule limits pine tar to 18 inches up the handle.

Tim McClelland lays the bat across the plate, finds tar well beyond the limit, and calls Brett out.

Brett comes out of the dugout in the eruption that became the photograph.

American League president Lee MacPhail overturns the call. The pine-tar rule, he writes, was about keeping the ball clean, not about canceling a home run after it had left the park. The game is resumed on August 18 from the moment after the homer, with Brett having been ejected for the argument and therefore not on the field. The Royals win, 5–4.

Martin had the rule on his side for an evening. MacPhail decided the rule had been pointed at the wrong thing. The resumed game took a few minutes. The argument took the rest of the summer.
counterfactual: MacPhail lets the out stand. Brett's homer stays off the board, and New York wins it the night it was played. There is no August 18 postscript, no resumption from the moment after the swing. The photograph of Brett leaving the dugout is still the photograph. The rule wins the argument it was written to win, even if it was pointed at the wrong thing.

title: Durham Lets It Through
summary: One out from a pennant that was already slipping away, Tim Flannery's grounder went through Leon Durham's legs. San Diego scored four and won the National League.
story:
October 7, 1984. Jack Murphy Stadium, Game 5, for the pennant.

The National League Championship Series is a best-of-five. The Cubs won the first two at Wrigley. San Diego won the next two at home. Rick Sutcliffe, who has barely lost since the Cubs acquired him in June, took a 3–0 lead to the middle innings. The Padres have cut it to 3–2.

In the seventh, Carmelo Martinez is on second with one out. Tim Flannery hits a grounder to first.

Leon Durham said afterward that it was a routine ball and it stayed low. It goes through his legs. Martinez scores. The inning comes apart. Tony Gwynn doubles, Steve Garvey singles, and San Diego scores four. The final is 6–3.

The Padres go to the World Series. The Cubs, who have not won a postseason series since 1908, go home.

A clubhouse story later claimed Durham's glove had been soaked by a spilled drink. He described a ball that never hopped. The grounder is enough.
counterfactual: Durham picks it. Martinez stays at second, and Sutcliffe — or whoever finishes — still has a 3–2 lead and a chance to send Chicago to the World Series. The Cubs might still have found another way to lose a pennant they had led two games to none. The grounder would not have been the way, and 1908 would have had to wait for some other ending.

damage.stakes: One out from a pennant that was already slipping away.

title: Denkinger Calls Orta Safe
summary: With St. Louis one out from a championship, Don Denkinger called Jorge Orta safe at first. Replays showed he was out. The Cardinals never got the inning back.
story:
October 26, 1985. Royals Stadium, Game 6.

The Cardinals lead 1–0 in the ninth and have not blown a ninth-inning lead all year. Todd Worrell is pitching. Jorge Orta, pinch-hitting, chops a ball to Jack Clark at first. Clark tosses to Worrell covering.

Don Denkinger, umpiring at first, calls Orta safe.

The replays show Worrell's foot on the bag about half a step ahead of Orta.

The inning does not end with the argument. Steve Balboni pops up a foul that Clark loses between himself, catcher Darrell Porter, and a camera near the dugout. Balboni then singles. Onix Concepcion runs for him. Jim Sundberg bunts, and Orta is forced at third. Porter's passed ball moves the runners up. Herzog walks Hal McRae on purpose. Dane Iorg, a former Cardinal, singles to right and scores both runners. Kansas City wins, 2–1.

The next day Denkinger is behind the plate for an 11–0 Game 7 in which Herzog and pitcher Joaquin Andujar are ejected. The call did not score the winning run by itself. Clark's missed pop-up, the passed ball, and Iorg's single happened after it. St. Louis spent the winter on the one that came first.
counterfactual: Denkinger calls him out. Worrell has the first out of the ninth, and what follows — Balboni's pop, the passed ball, Iorg's single — never gets the chance to happen. St. Louis wins, 1–0, and wins the Series that night. Denkinger works the next game, if there is one, as an umpire rather than a name. The winter in St. Louis is about a championship, not a call.

title: The Ball Gets Through Buckner
summary: The Red Sox were one out from a title when a ground ball went through Bill Buckner's legs. By then the lead was already gone.
story:
October 25, 1986. Shea Stadium, the tenth inning.

Vin Scully's voice is still the one you hear before you see the ball.

Two outs. Boston leads the World Series three games to two, and this game 5–4. One strike from the championship they have not held since 1918. Mookie Wilson fouls off pitch after pitch. John McNamara brings in Bob Stanley. What is scored a wild pitch — Rich Gedman in the middle of it — lets Kevin Mitchell come home and sends Ray Knight to second.

The game is tied before anyone hits it to first. Then the little roller, up along the line.

> So the winning run is at second base, with two outs, three and two to Mookie Wilson. Little roller up along first. Behind the bag! It gets through Buckner! Here comes Knight, and the Mets win it!

The ball never touches the glove. Knight comes around. Shea detonates. The series is even. Rain takes Sunday with it. On Monday the Mets finish what the tenth began.

Bill Buckner had 2,715 hits and a batting title. He was playing on bad ankles. Dave Stapleton had taken his place for defense in the late innings of every Red Sox win this postseason. McNamara left him out there. None of that changes the picture the night left behind: a ball between two legs, a runner crossing the plate, a title that had been one strike away and then was not.
counterfactual: The glove closes. Buckner steps on the bag, and the score is still 5–4. Boston wins Game 6 at Shea and wins the World Series that night, four games to two. Sixty-eight years end in a visiting clubhouse, not in a photograph. The photograph never exists. Buckner's career is told the ordinary way — the hits, the batting title, the ankles. The Curse ends in 1986, or it waits for some other night to break a city's heart. The record, of course, is otherwise.

title: Bagwell for Larry Andersen
summary: At the 1990 deadline the Red Sox traded a Double-A third baseman for a month of Larry Andersen. The third baseman was Jeff Bagwell.
story:
August 30, 1990. Boston needs a bullpen arm for a pennant race.

The Red Sox send minor-league third baseman Jeff Bagwell to Houston for reliever Larry Andersen. Andersen is 37. Bagwell is 22, blocked in the Red Sox system, and a lifelong Red Sox fan who does not want to go.

Andersen pitches in 15 games, posts a 1.23 ERA, and helps Boston win the American League East. He is a free agent that winter and signs with San Diego. Boston is out in the playoffs.

Bagwell becomes a first baseman because Houston already has Ken Caminiti at third. He is the National League Rookie of the Year in 1991, the Most Valuable Player in 1994, and finishes with 449 home runs.

The trade is the deadline deal against which other deadline deals are measured, because the rental worked and the prospect was still the greater player by an order the standings could not show in September.

Boston's need was real. The price was a player the club did not yet know it had.
counterfactual: Boston keeps the third baseman. Andersen is someone else's rental. The 1.23 ERA in 15 games never helps the 1990 club, and the 449 home runs never leave New England. Houston finds another first baseman. The deadline still happens every August; it has a different measuring stick.

damage.stakes: A deadline trade of a minor leaguer for a month of relief pitching.

title: Steve Lyons Drops His Pants
summary: Steve Lyons beat out a bunt, slid into first, and unbuckled his pants on live television to shake the dirt out.
story:
July 16, 1990. Tiger Stadium.

Steve Lyons — the White Sox utility man whose nickname was Psycho — leads off the fifth with a bunt single against Dan Petry and slides into the bag. While Petry argues with first baseman Cecil Fielder, Lyons feels the dirt in his uniform and does the thing a person does in a backyard: he unbuckles his pants to shake it out.

He gets them to his knees, remembers the crowd and the broadcast, and hauls them back up. He is wearing sliding shorts. Nobody is hurt.

The clip outlived almost everything else he did on a baseball field, which is its own small injustice and also the reason it is in the catalog. Lyons later became a broadcaster and told the story on himself, which is the decent version of this kind of moment.

It is here as a personality entry, not as a moral one. The sport has room for a man who forgot, for three seconds, that he was not alone.

title: Lonnie Smith Stops at Third
summary: In a scoreless Game 7, Lonnie Smith was on first when Terry Pendleton doubled. A decoy at second base held him at third. He never scored.
story:
October 27, 1991. The Metrodome, Game 7 of the World Series.

Jack Morris and John Smoltz have matched zeros into the eighth. Lonnie Smith leads off with a single. Terry Pendleton drives the ball into the left-center gap, the kind of hit the Atlanta dugout greets as a run. Smith is running on the pitch.

Near second he slows.

Chuck Knoblauch and Greg Gagne mime the turn of a double play, as if the ball were on the infield. It is not. It is on the warning track. Smith said later that he had not picked the ball up and that the decoy fooled him. By the time he sees it, third is all he can reach.

Ron Gant grounds out. David Justice walks. Sid Bream grounds into a 3-2-3 double play, Kent Hrbek to Brian Harper to Hrbek. The inning dies with the run on third.

Morris finishes ten shutout innings. In the bottom of the tenth Dan Gladden doubles, Knoblauch sacrifices, the Twins walk Kirby Puckett and Hrbek intentionally, and the injured Gene Larkin singles home the winner on the first pitch he sees from Alejandro Peña. Minnesota wins, 1–0.

Smith called it his mistake. The series is remembered as one of the best ever played. His hesitation is the reason it went to the tenth at all.
counterfactual: Smith never buys the decoy. He scores, or at least he is waved home with a play at the plate, and Atlanta has the lead in the eighth of a scoreless Game 7. Morris might still have answered. Peña might still have been the pitcher in the tenth. Or the Braves close it before Larkin ever comes to the plate. The hesitation never becomes the reason a 1–0 game needed extra innings.

title: The Ball Comes Off Canseco's Head
summary: Carlos Martinez flew to right at Cleveland Stadium. The ball ticked Jose Canseco's glove, hit him on the head, and bounced over the fence for a home run.
story:
May 26, 1993. Cleveland Stadium, the Rangers in town and leading 3–0.

In the bottom of the fourth Carlos Martinez leads off with a fly to right. Jose Canseco drifts back, turns his head to find the wall, and loses the ball. It grazes his glove, strikes him on the top of the head, and bounces over the fence.

By rule it is a home run. Center fielder David Hulse, backing up the play, is laughing before Martinez has rounded second.

Cleveland wins, 7–6. Canseco, who understood the clip would be everywhere, asked if anybody had a Band-Aid and said he would be on television for a month. He was right about the month.

The play is funny in the way a baseball blooper is funny, and it is also a perfect small fielding entry: an outfielder looking for the fence instead of the ball, and the ball finding him anyway.

Martinez, whose homer it officially was, said he thought Canseco had it, and then he saw it hit him. That is the whole sequence. It does not need a second act.

title: Pedro Martinez for Delino DeShields
summary: The Dodgers needed a second baseman and traded Pedro Martinez to Montreal to get one. Pedro became one of the great pitchers of the era.
story:
November 19, 1993. The Dodgers trade Pedro Martinez to the Expos for second baseman Delino DeShields.

Los Angeles has failed to re-sign Jody Reed and wants an everyday second baseman. Martinez is 22, listed at 5-foot-11, a year removed from shoulder surgery, and has just gone 10–5 with a 2.61 ERA as a reliever. The club is not sure the arm will hold up as a starter. DeShields is a former first-round pick who can run and hit at the top of an order.

DeShields is a useful Dodger and not a disaster. Martinez becomes a three-time Cy Young winner and, for a few seasons in Boston, the best pitcher alive.

The trade looks inevitable only after those seasons. In November 1993 it was a team choosing a position it could see an opening at, and declining to bet that a small right-hander coming off shoulder surgery was the more valuable asset.

They chose wrong. The useful part of the record is that the choice had reasons. The reasons were not good enough.
counterfactual: Los Angeles keeps the small right-hander. DeShields remains an Expo. The Cy Young seasons, if the arm holds, belong to the club that was not sure it would. Montreal's good teams of the mid-nineties have to win without him — or they become even harder to beat. The second-base opening is filled some other way.

damage.stakes: A young pitcher traded for the second baseman the club wanted that year.

title: Albert Belle's Corked Bat
summary: Umpires confiscated Albert Belle's bat in Chicago. A teammate crawled through the ceiling to swap it, and the replacement had the wrong name on it.
story:
July 15, 1994. Cleveland at Chicago.

The umpires take Albert Belle's bat out of the game before he can use it. What happens next is the part the players later told on themselves. Pitcher Jason Grimsley crawls through the crawlspace above the clubhouse ceiling, drops into the umpires' room, and replaces the confiscated bat with one belonging to teammate Paul Sorrento.

The switch does not survive a look at the barrel. The bat in the umpires' care is not Belle's model. The bat they had originally taken was corked. Belle is suspended seven games.

Cork in a bat is an old trick, illegal because it lightens the barrel and changes how the ball comes off it. The ceiling crawl is what separated this one from a routine suspension.

Belle was the hitter. Grimsley was the operation. The rule is simple enough that the ingenuity spent getting around it is the embarrassing half of the story.

title: Jeffrey Maier Reaches Over the Wall
summary: A twelve-year-old reached over the wall and turned Derek Jeter's fly ball into a home run. The umpire out there never saw the hand.
story:
October 9, 1996. Yankee Stadium, Game 1 of the American League Championship Series.

In the eighth inning Derek Jeter, a rookie, flies to right. Tony Tarasco camps under it. Jeffrey Maier, twelve years old and sitting in the front row, reaches over the wall with his glove and deflects the ball into the stands.

Right-field umpire Rich Garcia signals a home run. The call ties the game. New York wins it later, and wins the series.

Garcia said, after he saw the replay, that he probably would have called fan interference. Tarasco did not accept the companion claim that he had no chance at the ball. The rule is plain: a spectator who reaches into the field of play and touches a ball that a fielder has a play on has interfered.

Maier was a child doing what children in the front row do. The missed call belonged to the umpire who was stationed there to see it.

Jeter's career made the homer look destined. On the night, it was a fly ball, a glove from the seats, and a signal that did not match the play.
counterfactual: Garcia sees the glove come over the wall. Interference. The ball is not a home run, and the game is not tied on a child's hand. Baltimore still has to finish the night. New York still might have won the series. The signal matches the play, and Tarasco's argument is the one the rule already agrees with.

title: Rick Ankiel Loses the Plate
summary: Rick Ankiel was twenty-one, a phenom, and ahead 6–0 in his first playoff start. In the third inning he threw five wild pitches and could not find the strike zone.
story:
October 3, 2000. National League Division Series Game 1, the Cardinals against the Braves in St. Louis.

Rick Ankiel is twenty-one and has just finished a rookie season in which he looked like one of the best young pitchers in the league. Tony La Russa hands him the ball. St. Louis scores six in the first. The choice looks like genius.

In the third inning the strike zone disappears.

Ankiel throws five wild pitches, walks four, and uses 34 pitches, 20 of them balls. Atlanta scores four. He had thrown twelve wild pitches in 175 regular-season innings. Five of them arrive in one playoff inning.

Baseball already had a name for this kind of sudden loss of command, after Steve Blass, the Pirates pitcher who won 19 games in 1972 and could not throw a strike in 1973. Ankiel's version arrived on television, in October, at 21.

He did not get the pitch back as a pitcher. He left the game for a time, came back as an outfielder, and had a real hitting career. The inning is in the catalog because it happened. It is not here as a joke about a young man whose arm stopped obeying him.

title: Byung-Hyun Kim, Two Nights
summary: Byung-Hyun Kim gave up a game-tying homer in the ninth on consecutive nights of the 2001 World Series. Arizona won the series anyway.
story:
October 31, 2001. Yankee Stadium, Game 4 of the World Series.

Arizona leads 3–1 in the ninth. Byung-Hyun Kim has struck out the side in the eighth, and Bob Brenly sends him back out. Paul O'Neill singles with one out. With two out, Tino Martinez hits a two-run homer, and the game is tied.

In the tenth, after midnight, Derek Jeter homers. The papers call him Mr. November. New York wins, 4–3. Kim is the losing pitcher.

The next night Arizona leads 2–0 in the ninth, and Brenly goes to Kim again. Jorge Posada leads off with a double. Kim retires the next two. Scott Brosius homers them both in, and the game is tied again. Alfonso Soriano singles home Chuck Knoblauch in the twelfth. New York wins, 3–2, and leads the series three games to two.

Arizona wins Games 6 and 7 in Phoenix anyway, the last of them on Luis Gonzalez's broken-bat single off Mariano Rivera. Kim's two nights did not cost his team the championship. They cost him the ninth inning twice, which is a narrower and more accurate thing to say. Brenly's decision to bring him back on the second night is part of the entry, not a footnote.

title: Castillo Drops the Popup
summary: The Mets led by a run with two outs in the ninth when Luis Castillo dropped Alex Rodriguez's popup, then threw to the wrong base.
story:
June 12, 2009. The new Yankee Stadium, the first Subway Series game there that year.

The Mets lead 8–7 in the ninth. David Wright's double off Mariano Rivera in the eighth has put them there. Francisco Rodriguez is one out from a save. Derek Jeter is on second, Mark Teixeira on first after an intentional walk, and Alex Rodriguez pops up a pitch he had been ahead in the count on.

Rodriguez slams his bat down. He thinks the game is over.

Luis Castillo, a three-time Gold Glove second baseman, drifts into short right and tries to take the ball one-handed. It hits the glove and falls. Jeter scores easily. Castillo then throws to second instead of home, and Teixeira scores too. The Yankees win, 9–8.

Castillo sat alone in the visitors' clubhouse afterward and said it was a routine fly ball, and that the ball was moving.

The Mets of that summer were already finding new ways to lose. This one was the plainest: two outs, a popup, a Gold Glove, and a throw that did not even try for the runner at the plate.
counterfactual: Two hands. The popup is an out. Rodriguez slams the bat and is right this time. The Mets win, 8–7, and take the first Subway Series game in the new building. Castillo is still a Gold Glover who caught a routine fly. The throw to the wrong base never has a reason to be made.

title: The Bartman Game
summary: Five outs from the World Series, a fan deflected a foul ball. The Cubs' shortstop then missed the double-play ball that would have ended the inning anyway.
story:
October 14, 2003. Wrigley Field, National League Championship Series Game 6.

The Cubs lead the series three games to two and the game 3–0 in the eighth. Mark Prior is pitching. Five outs remain. Juan Pierre doubles. Luis Castillo, on a full count, fouls a ball down the left-field line.

Moises Alou reaches the wall. Several fans reach too. Steve Bartman, headphones on, eyes on the ball, deflects it. Left-field umpire Mike Everitt does not call interference. Alou slams his glove.

Prior's next pitch is wild. Castillo walks. Ivan Rodriguez singles, and it is 3–1. Miguel Cabrera then hits a grounder to shortstop Alex Gonzalez — a tailor-made double play — and Gonzalez boots it. Derrek Lee doubles and the game is tied. The Marlins score eight runs in the inning and win, 8–3. Five of those runs are unearned because of Gonzalez. Florida wins Game 7 the next night.

Alou later said he did not believe the foul ball was fan interference. In 2016 the Cubs gave Bartman a World Series ring. The entry keeps his name because that is what the night was called. The play that actually reopened the inning was a baseball play: a shortstop missing a grounder with runners on first and second and one out.
counterfactual: The fans pull back. Alou has a play. If he squeezes it, there are four outs to go and a 3–0 lead, and Gonzalez never sees that grounder. The Cubs still have to win Game 6, and then Game 7. Bartman goes home unknown. The shortstop's error, if it still happens on some other ball, is the baseball play the night actually turned on — without a fan's name attached to it.

title: Grady Little Leaves Pedro In
summary: Boston led Game 7 of the 2003 ALCS by three runs. Grady Little visited the mound, left a tiring Pedro Martinez in, and the Yankees tied the game.
story:
October 16, 2003. Yankee Stadium, Game 7 of the American League Championship Series.

The Red Sox lead 5–2 in the eighth. Pedro Martinez has already thrown well past 100 pitches and is laboring. The bullpen is up. Grady Little walks to the mound, talks to his pitcher, and leaves him in.

Derek Jeter doubles. Bernie Williams singles. Hideki Matsui doubles. Jorge Posada doubles home the tying runs.

The game goes to the eleventh, where Aaron Boone hits a walk-off homer off Tim Wakefield. Little's contract is not renewed. The Red Sox win the World Series the next year with a different manager, which turned this night into the preface of a revenge story.

On the night itself it was a lead, a tired ace, and a visit that did not include a pitching change.

Leaving Pedro in was not irrational. He was Pedro Martinez. It was still the decision, and the next four hitters were the evidence.
counterfactual: Little takes the ball. The bullpen inherits a 5–2 lead with four outs to get. Jeter, Williams, Matsui, and Posada face someone else. Boone may never come to the plate in the eleventh. Little still has to manage the rest of a Game 7. He does not become the man who left Pedro in, and the next year does not have to arrive as revenge.

damage.stakes: Game 7 of the championship series. Boston led by three when the manager reached the mound.

title: Galarraga's Imperfect Game
summary: Armando Galarraga was one out from a perfect game when Jim Joyce called Jason Donald safe. Joyce saw the replay, and said he had missed it.
story:
June 2, 2010. Comerica Park.

Armando Galarraga has retired the first 26 Cleveland hitters. Jason Donald grounds to first. Miguel Cabrera fields it and throws to Galarraga covering the bag. Donald is out, plainly, on the replay everyone in the park can see a moment later.

Jim Joyce, umpiring at first, calls him safe.

Galarraga smiles, takes the ball back, and gets the next batter. Detroit wins the game. Joyce watches the replay in the umpires' room and comes out in tears. He says he has blown the call and that he has cost the kid a perfect game. The next afternoon Galarraga carries the lineup card to the plate and the two men embrace.

Commissioner Bud Selig does not overturn the out. A perfect game is a historical category with a definition, and the definition still said Donald had reached.

The missed call is why the game is in a catalog of blunders. The apology, and the way it was received, are why the entry cannot stop at the call. Joyce did not hide from the replay. Galarraga did not make him.
counterfactual: Joyce's hand goes up. Donald is out. Galarraga has a perfect game — the twenty-seventh in a row — and the historical category matches what everyone in the park saw. There is no lineup-card embrace the next day. There does not need to be. Selig never has a call to leave alone.

title: The Infield Fly in Atlanta
summary: With the Braves rallying in a winner-take-all game, Sam Holbrook called the infield fly rule on a ball that fell in short left field. The crowd threw trash for nineteen minutes.
story:
October 5, 2012. Turner Field, the first National League Wild Card game, and Chipper Jones's last.

The Cardinals lead 6–3. In the bottom of the eighth, Atlanta has runners on first and second with one out. On a 3–2 pitch from Mitchell Boggs, Andrelton Simmons pops a ball into short left. Shortstop Pete Kozma drifts well onto the grass. Left fielder Matt Holliday comes in. Neither catches it.

Left-field umpire Sam Holbrook has invoked the infield fly rule. Simmons is out. The runners stay at first and second. The ball has landed something like ninety feet beyond the infield dirt.

Holbrook said he had seen the shortstop get under it with ordinary effort, which is the rule's actual test: not where the ball lands, but whether an infielder can catch it without undue trouble. Joe Torre, then running baseball operations, denied Atlanta's protest because a judgment call cannot be protested.

Fans throw bottles and cups onto the field. The delay lasts nineteen minutes, and the public address warns that the game could be forfeited. St. Louis wins, 6–3, and goes on to the World Series.

The call could be both legal and absurd to everyone watching it. That is the entry.
counterfactual: Holbrook keeps the call in his pocket. The ball is in play. Atlanta has a chance to score without an out appearing from a rule, and the protest is never filed. Nineteen minutes of trash never happen. St. Louis might still have won, 6–3. The last image of Chipper Jones's last game would not be a rulebook argument.
