title: Chesbro's Wild Pitch
summary: Jack Chesbro had already won 41 games. In the ninth of the pennant game, a spitball got past his catcher, and Boston scored the run that ended it.
story:
October 10, 1904. Hilltop Park, the first game of a doubleheader.

The Highlanders trail the Boston Americans by a game and a half and need both games. The score is tied, 2–2, in the ninth, with two out and Lou Criger on third. Freddy Parent has two strikes. Jack Chesbro, who will finish 41–12, throws the spitball that has carried him all year.

The pitch gets past catcher Red Kleinow. It is scored a wild pitch. Criger comes home, and Boston leads, 3–2. Bill Dinneen, the winning pitcher, holds the lead. The pennant race is over.

Clark Griffith, the Highlanders' manager, said Kleinow had simply let the ball get away, which would have made it a passed ball. The official record did not agree with him.

Chesbro's season remains the modern record for wins. The last of them was not this game. The retelling sometimes treats the pitch as the only thing that separated New York from a pennant. They were already behind in the standings when they took the field.
counterfactual: Kleinow holds it. Criger stays at third. Parent still has two strikes, and Chesbro still has to finish the at-bat. New York still has to win two games while already behind in the standings. The spitball is just another pitch in a 41-win season. It is not the last word of the race.

damage.stakes: Two out in the ninth of the pennant game, the score tied, a runner on third.

title: The Double No-Hitter Breaks
summary: Hippo Vaughn and Fred Toney both pitched nine no-hit innings. In the tenth, a single, a dropped fly, and a throw home the catcher was not looking for ended it.
story:
May 2, 1917. Weeghman Park, later Wrigley Field.

Hippo Vaughn of the Cubs and Fred Toney of the Reds retire the first twenty-seven men they face. Vaughn has walked two, and both were erased on double plays. Through nine innings the score is 0–0, and neither side has a hit.

In the tenth, Larry Kopf singles between Larry Doyle and Fred Merkle for the game's first hit. Cy Williams drops Hal Chase's line drive. Chase steals second. Jim Thorpe then tops a ball up the third-base line.

Vaughn throws home. Catcher Art Wilson is looking for a throw to first. The ball hits him, and Kopf scores. Wilson recovers in time to tag Chase.

Toney then finishes the tenth without a hit. The Reds win, 1–0. Vaughn said afterward that he had grown careless on Kopf.

The game is remembered as the double no-hitter, which is almost right: two men pitched nine hitless innings, and only one of them was allowed to finish the tenth that way.

title: Ruth Is Out at Second
summary: The 1926 World Series ended with Babe Ruth thrown out at second. He said he was stealing on his own. Other accounts say a hit-and-run was on.
story:
October 10, 1926. Yankee Stadium, Game 7.

The Cardinals lead, 3–2. Grover Cleveland Alexander, who pitched a complete game the day before, came in during the seventh with the bases loaded and two out. Tony Lazzeri fouled one just foul down the left-field line and then struck out.

In the ninth Alexander retires Earle Combs and Mark Koenig and walks Babe Ruth, his fourth walk of the game. Ruth had homered in the fourth. Bob Meusel is at bat. Lou Gehrig is on deck.

Ruth runs on a pitch. Bob O'Farrell throws to Rogers Hornsby, and Ruth is out.

It is still the only World Series to end on a caught stealing. The box score is not in dispute. The reason for the run is.

Ruth said after the game that he had gone on his own, to reach scoring position if Meusel hit. Other writers, including accounts in The Sporting News, said a hit-and-run was on and that Meusel had swung and missed. The later story sometimes adds that Alexander was hung over. Nothing in the contemporary record establishes that, and the play does not need it.
counterfactual: Ruth stays put. Meusel hits, or he does not; Gehrig still waits on deck. The Series does not end on a caught stealing, the only one that ever has. Alexander still has to get someone out. Hornsby does not apply the last tag of October.

damage.stakes: Game 7, the Cardinals led by a run in the ninth. Gehrig was on deck.

title: Slaughter Scores from First
summary: Enos Slaughter scored from first on Harry Walker's double in Game 7. The relay went through Johnny Pesky, who said he hesitated. Later viewings say the run was coming anyway.
story:
October 15, 1946. Sportsman's Park, Game 7, attendance 36,143.

The score is tied, 3–3, in the eighth after Dom DiMaggio's double. DiMaggio pulls a muscle and is replaced by Leon Culberson. In the bottom of the inning Enos Slaughter singles to open against Bob Klinger. Two outs follow. Slaughter is running on a hit-and-run when Harry Walker doubles to center.

Culberson relays the ball to Johnny Pesky in short left-center. Third-base coach Mike Gonzalez waves Slaughter home. The Cardinals lead, 4–3, and hold it. Harry Brecheen is the winning pitcher in relief.

Jerry Nason, writing in the Boston Globe, said Pesky froze and pivoted slowly. Pesky said after the game that he had hesitated because he thought Slaughter would hold at third.

The phrase that stuck was that Pesky held the ball. Later film and later accounts, including Joe Posnanski's, describe a brief double-clutch, with Walker already at second by the time Pesky had the ball and Slaughter going to score either way. The hesitation is in Pesky's own account. The several seconds of the legend are not.
counterfactual: Culberson makes a stronger throw, or Pesky turns and fires without the double-clutch, and there is a play at the plate. Slaughter might still have been safe — later film says he was going to score either way. Or he is out, the game stays 3–3, and Game 7 goes to the ninth. The phrase "Pesky held the ball" never outruns the film.

damage.stakes: Game 7, eighth inning, the score tied. He was on first when the ball was hit to center.

title: Twelve Perfect Innings
summary: Harvey Haddix retired 36 batters in a row and lost in the thirteenth. Joe Adcock's ball cleared the fence, and the next day the league president made it a double.
story:
May 26, 1959. County Stadium.

Harvey Haddix of the Pirates retires the first thirty-six Milwaukee Braves. Lew Burdette matches him with zeros, though not with a perfect game.

In the thirteenth, Felix Mantilla, who entered in the tenth, leads off with a grounder to Don Hoak. The throw is in the dirt, and Rocky Nelson cannot scoop it. Error. Eddie Mathews sacrifices Mantilla to second. Hank Aaron is walked intentionally.

Joe Adcock drives a pitch over the fence in right-center. Aaron, thinking the ball has stayed in the park, touches second and cuts across the diamond toward the dugout. Adcock passes him and is ruled out, so the hit becomes a double. Umpires first allow more than one run. The next day National League president Warren Giles rules the score 1–0. Once the hit is a double, only the run needed to end the game counts.

Haddix is the losing pitcher. He had one hit against him, one intentional walk, and an unearned run. He said afterward that twelve perfect innings had seemed, to him, like just another loss. He had not known it was unprecedented.

The record book could not decide, for a night, what the ball over the fence had been. The loss never needed the help.

damage.stakes: He had retired thirty-six in a row. The perfect game and the game itself ended in the thirteenth.

title: Three Errors in One Inning
summary: In the fifth inning of World Series Game 2, Willie Davis lost two fly balls in the sun and threw one away. Three errors, three unearned runs, and Jim Palmer's shutout.
story:
October 6, 1966. Dodger Stadium, Game 2, attendance 55,947.

Sandy Koufax starts for Los Angeles. Jim Palmer, twenty years old, starts for Baltimore. In the top of the fifth Willie Davis loses two flies in the sun and throws a ball past third.

Three errors in one inning, a World Series record, and three unearned runs.

The Orioles add more later, including a run in the sixth off Koufax. Los Angeles makes six errors in the game. Palmer finishes a four-hit shutout. Koufax works six innings, allows one earned run, and takes the loss. The final is 6–0.

The series is remembered for Baltimore's pitching. This inning is the other half of that memory: a center fielder losing the ball in the sun, twice, in the same inning he also threw one away. The runs were unearned. The shutout still counted.

title: A Black Cat at Shea
summary: A black cat walked in front of the Cubs' dugout at Shea. Chicago lost, 7–1. The standings, not the cat, are what the collapse was.
story:
September 9, 1969. Shea Stadium, attendance 51,448.

The Cubs lead the National League East by a game and a half. On August 19 the lead had been eight games. Tom Seaver starts for the Mets. Ferguson Jenkins starts for Chicago.

In the top of the fourth, with Glenn Beckert on second and Ron Santo in the on-deck circle, a black cat comes onto the field, walks in front of the Cubs' dugout, and disappears under the stands.

Santo said years later that the cat had looked at Leo Durocher. Ed Kranepool said Shea had a lot of rats, and therefore a lot of cats. After the cat leaves, Santo singles home the Cubs' only run. Seaver beats Jenkins, 7–1. Chicago's lead is down to half a game.

The Cubs go 8–17 in September. The Mets go 23–7 and clinch the division on September 24. Durocher's refusal to rest regulars is the explanation that shows up in the later accounts. The cat is the picture. It did not change the score.

title: Seaver to Cincinnati
summary: On the night of the trading deadline, the Mets sent Tom Seaver to Cincinnati for four players, and Dave Kingman to San Diego in a separate deal.
story:
June 15, 1977. Deadline night.

The Mets, in last place, send Tom Seaver to the Cincinnati Reds for Pat Zachry, Doug Flynn, Steve Henderson, and Dan Norman. The same night they send Dave Kingman, the club's home-run leader, to the San Diego Padres for Bobby Valentine and Paul Siebert. Chairman M. Donald Grant and Seaver have been feuding in the papers for months over Seaver's contract.

The New York Times describes the return for Seaver as four players of far less magnitude. Henderson becomes a useful major leaguer. The night itself does not look like an even trade, and the papers do not treat it as one. The deal ends weeks of speculation and begins a rebuild the club had not announced as a plan.

It is filed with the Ruth sale and the Ryan trade because the shape is the same: a franchise pitcher leaves, the public case for the return is thin, and the argument afterward is about what the club thought it was doing. Grant's side of the feud was about money and authority. The box score of the trade is the four names.

title: Dent over the Monster
summary: In the one-game playoff at Fenway, Bucky Dent, batting ninth, hit a three-run homer over the Green Monster. He had borrowed Mickey Rivers's bat after fouling a pitch off his foot.
story:
October 2, 1978. Fenway Park, attendance 32,925, a one-game playoff for the American League East.

The Red Sox had held a double-digit lead in July. They lead this game, 2–0, after Carl Yastrzemski's homer in the second. In the seventh, with two out and Chris Chambliss and Roy White on base, Bucky Dent comes up. He is hitting ninth. It is his fifth home run of the year.

He fouls a pitch off his foot. During the delay he borrows a bat from Mickey Rivers. Mike Torrez, who later said he took no warm-up pitches after the stoppage, throws again.

Dent hits it to left, over the wall. The Yankees lead, 3–2.

Rivers then walks, steals second, and Thurman Munson doubles him home before Torrez comes out for Bob Stanley. Reggie Jackson homers in the eighth. Boston scores twice in the eighth and loses, 5–4. Ron Guidry gets the win. Rich Gossage gets the save.

The nickname that followed Dent around Boston is the retelling. The play was a home run by a .243 shortstop, on a borrowed bat, in a game both clubs had spent two months reaching.
counterfactual: The ball dies at the wall, or it never leaves the infield. Chambliss and White stay on base with two out, and Boston still leads, 2–0, in a one-game playoff it had spent two months earning. Torrez might still have had to get someone else. Guidry might still have been the better pitcher that afternoon. Dent goes back to hitting ninth, without a nickname waiting for him in Boston.

damage.stakes: A one-game playoff. Boston led by two with two out in the seventh.

title: Randle Blows It Foul
summary: Lenny Randle dropped to the Kingdome turf and blew a slow roller across the foul line. The umpire called it foul, then changed the call after the Royals protested.
story:
May 27, 1981. The Kingdome.

Amos Otis of the Kansas City Royals taps a ball toward third that keeps rolling on the artificial turf. Mariners third baseman Lenny Randle goes to his hands and knees and blows on it until it crosses the foul line. Home-plate umpire Larry McCoy calls the ball foul.

Royals manager Jim Frey protests. McCoy reverses himself and sends Otis to first.

Randle's explanation was that he had been talking to the ball.

> I said, "Please go foul, go foul." I did not blow on it. I just used the power of suggestion.

The film does not support the second sentence.

The Royals win the game, 8–5. That score is not why the play is here. A fielder tried to move a live ball with his breath, an umpire allowed it, and then the same umpire took it back. The rulebook had no provision for either half.

title: Perry, Ejected
summary: Dave Phillips ejected Gaylord Perry for a spitball without looking at the ball. Perry said it was a forkball. The league suspended him for ten days anyway.
story:
August 23, 1982. The Kingdome, Mariners against the Red Sox.

Gaylord Perry is forty-three and in his twenty-first season, with a long reputation for doctoring baseballs and, until this night, no ejection for it. In the fifth, home-plate umpire Dave Phillips checks a ball, says he has found a slippery foreign substance, and warns Perry. Phillips says he is not a chemist and does not know what the substance is.

In the seventh, with Rick Miller batting and runners on first and third, Miller swings and misses a 1–0 pitch. Phillips ejects Perry without asking for the ball. He says the flight was enough, and that the rule allowed him to judge an illegal pitch that way.

Perry says he has thrown a hard forkball, that Phillips had no evidence, and that if anything had been on the earlier ball the umpire had put it there. He also says the trouble started in the first inning, over two pitches to Carl Yastrzemski.

American League president Lee MacPhail suspends Perry for ten days and fines him $250. The penalty is stayed while Perry appeals, then upheld. Perry never said, that night, whether the pitch was doctored. The ejection rests on an umpire's reading of a baseball he did not keep.

title: Lasorda Pitches to Clark
summary: With first base open in the ninth of the 1985 NLCS, Tommy Lasorda let Tom Niedenfuer pitch to Jack Clark. Clark hit the first pitch into the left-field seats.
story:
October 16, 1985. Dodger Stadium, Game 6 of the National League Championship Series, attendance 55,208.

The Dodgers lead, 5–4, in the ninth. Tom Niedenfuer is in to protect the lead and force a seventh game. Tommy Lasorda has him walk Ozzie Smith. A groundout leaves runners on second and third with two out. First base is open. Jack Clark is the hitter. Andy Van Slyke, who has not been the threat Clark was in the series, is on deck.

Lasorda has ordered Clark walked the last three times he has come up with a runner in scoring position and first base open. This time he pitches to him.

Clark hits the first pitch, a fastball, into the left-field bleachers. The Cardinals win, 7–5, and the pennant, four games to two. Niedenfuer takes the loss.

Lasorda said afterward that it was the easiest thing in the world, after the fact, to say he should have walked Clark, and that a deep fly caught for the third out would have produced the opposite argument. The decision is in the entry because it was a choice, stated at the time, between an open base and a hitter. The home run is what the choice became.
counterfactual: Lasorda holds up four fingers. Clark goes to first. Van Slyke has to beat Niedenfuer with the pennant on the line. He might have. A deep fly might have ended it the other way, as Lasorda said. The first-pitch fastball never leaves the park. The series goes to a seventh game.

damage.stakes: Game 6, two out in the ninth, first base open. A walk would have brought up the next hitter.

title: Hawkins Loses a No-Hitter
summary: Andy Hawkins allowed no hits and lost, 4–0, on three errors in the eighth. A year later baseball decided eight innings was not a no-hitter.
story:
July 1, 1990. Old Comiskey Park.

The Yankees are the visitors, so a Chicago win will end the game after eight. Andy Hawkins has not allowed a hit. In the eighth, with two out and the bases loaded, rookie catcher Jim Leyritz drops Robin Ventura's fly in left. Three runs score. Jesse Barfield, the right fielder, then loses Ivan Calderon's fly in the sun and drops it. Ventura scores.

The White Sox win, 4–0. Hawkins is the losing pitcher. Barry Jones gets the win. The Yankees have three errors. Chicago has no hits.

At the time the game is treated as a no-hitter, the sixth of a season that has just produced two on the same night, by Dave Stewart and Fernando Valenzuela, both of them wins. Hawkins had been close to release three weeks earlier.

In 1991 a committee under Commissioner Fay Vincent defines a no-hitter as nine innings or more. Games shorter than that become "notable achievements." Hawkins's line is removed from the list. The hits did not change. The name of the game did.

title: Carter off Williams
summary: Mitch Williams came in to protect a one-run lead in Game 6. He walked Rickey Henderson, gave up a single to Paul Molitor, and Joe Carter hit the next well-struck pitch over the left-field fence.
story:
October 23, 1993. SkyDome, Game 6, attendance 52,195.

The Phillies lead, 6–5, and a win would force a seventh game. Jim Fregosi brings in Mitch Williams, who had 43 saves that season and had already been scored on heavily in Game 4. The ninth begins with Williams, working from the stretch, nearly throwing a pitch after time has been called. He holds the ball and falls off toward the first-base side.

He walks Rickey Henderson on four pitches. Devon White flies out. Paul Molitor singles, sending Henderson to second. Joe Carter, ahead in the count and then even at 2–2, hits a pitch over the left-field fence.

Williams called it a mistake, a pitch that was supposed to be up and away. Fregosi remembered a bad slider. Carter said he lost the ball in the lights and knew only that it had the height. The Blue Jays win, 8–6.

It was the second walk-off home run to end a World Series, after Bill Mazeroski's in 1960, and the first of them hit while the home team trailed. The retelling begins and ends with the swing. The inning had already included a walk to the league's best base runner and a single by the man who had homered earlier in the game.
counterfactual: The slider is up and away, or it is a ball, or Carter hits it at someone. Philadelphia holds, 6–5, and there is a Game 7. Williams still has 43 saves and a rough Game 4. He is not the man on the wrong end of the second walk-off homer to end a World Series. Henderson's walk is just a leadoff walk, not the first domino.

damage.stakes: Game 6, ninth inning, a one-run lead. A win would have forced a seventh game.

title: Mesa in the Ninth
summary: The Indians led Game 7 by a run in the ninth. Jose Mesa allowed the tying sacrifice fly. Edgar Renteria's winning single, two innings later, came off Charles Nagy.
story:
October 26, 1997. Pro Player Stadium, Game 7, attendance 67,204.

Cleveland leads, 2–1, going to the bottom of the ninth. Jose Mesa, the Indians' closer, comes on. Moises Alou singles. Charles Johnson singles, sending Alou to third. Craig Counsell's sacrifice fly to right scores Alou. The game is tied, 2–2.

It stays tied through the tenth. In the eleventh, Bobby Bonilla singles, and Counsell reaches on an error by second baseman Tony Fernandez. Charles Nagy, who had started, is now pitching. With two out, Edgar Renteria singles to center. Counsell scores. The run is unearned. Florida wins, 3–2, in its fifth season.

Mesa is the name attached to the loss, and the tying run is his. The run that ended the series was not. Fernandez's error put Counsell on, and Nagy threw the pitch Renteria hit. The entry is the ninth inning and the two innings that followed it, not a single closer's line.

title: Roberts Steals Second
summary: Down three games to none and a run in the ninth, the Red Sox sent Dave Roberts in to run. He stole second against Mariano Rivera, and Bill Mueller singled him home.
story:
October 17, 2004. Fenway Park, Game 4 of the American League Championship Series.

The Yankees lead the series three games to none and the game, 4–3, in the ninth. Mariano Rivera is pitching. Kevin Millar walks. Dave Roberts comes in to run for him.

Roberts steals second.

Bill Mueller singles to center, and Roberts scores the tying run. The game goes to the twelfth, where David Ortiz wins it. Boston wins the next three games as well. No club had come back from a three-games-to-none deficit in a league championship series.

The steal is a baserunning play, not a mistake by the runner. It is in this catalog because of the situation it interrupted: the inning of a pitcher who had been close to automatic, with the series one game from over, and a pinch runner put on base for the single purpose of taking the next one. Rivera had already walked the leadoff man. The stolen base made the walk into the tying run.
counterfactual: The throw gets him. Rivera finishes the ninth. New York wins, 4–3, and wins the series the way a three-games-to-none lead is supposed to end. Ortiz never sees the twelfth. The 2004 Red Sox do not become the club that came back from the dead. They become another club that got close.

damage.stakes: Down three games to none, and a run, in the ninth. The steal tied the game.

title: The Ball over Cruz
summary: With two outs in the ninth of World Series Game 6, David Freese's ball went over Nelson Cruz's head and tied the game. Texas led again in the tenth. St. Louis won in the eleventh.
story:
October 27, 2011. Busch Stadium, Game 6.

The Rangers lead, 7–5, in the bottom of the ninth, two outs from a championship. Neftali Feliz is pitching. Ryan Theriot strikes out. Albert Pujols doubles. Lance Berkman walks. Allen Craig strikes out.

David Freese then hits a ball into right field, over Nelson Cruz, for a two-run triple. The game is tied, 7–7.

In the tenth Josh Hamilton homers, and Texas leads, 9–7. St. Louis scores once and then ties it again on Berkman's single. In the eleventh Freese leads off with a home run against Mark Lowe. The Cardinals win, 10–9. They win Game 7 the next night.

Cruz did not drop a ball he had caught. The triple went over his head, which is a different play and, in the retelling, the same one: the right fielder at the moment the lead disappeared. The game had a second lead after that, and a walk-off that was not his to field.
counterfactual: Cruz gets back. The ball is an out — two outs already in, the third one that would have ended it — or it is a single that does not score two. Texas wins, 7–5, and wins the Series that night in St. Louis. Freese never comes to the plate in the eleventh. Hamilton's homer in the tenth is never needed.

damage.stakes: Game 6, one out left in the ninth. Texas led by two.

title: Davis off Chapman
summary: Joe Maddon brought Aroldis Chapman in to protect a three-run lead in the eighth inning of Game 7. Rajai Davis hit a two-run homer that tied it. The Cubs won in the tenth.
story:
November 2, 2016. Progressive Field, Game 7.

The Cubs lead, 6–3, in the eighth. Joe Maddon brings in Aroldis Chapman, the closer, with a three-run lead and six outs still to get if the ninth is going to be his as well.

Rajai Davis hits a two-run homer. The game is tied, 6–6.

A rain delay follows. In the tenth Ben Zobrist and Miguel Montero drive in runs, Cleveland scores once, and the Cubs win, 8–7. It ends a World Series drought that had lasted since 1908.

The homer did not lose the series. It tied a game Chicago still won. What the entry keeps is the choice to spend Chapman in the eighth, up three, and the pitch that made the lead disappear for an inning and a delay. Davis earned the home run. The managerial part is when the pitcher was asked to get those outs.
counterfactual: Davis's ball stays in the park. Chapman finishes the eighth, and maybe the ninth. The Cubs win, 6–3, without a rain delay or a tenth inning. The drought still ends. It ends quieter, and Chapman is the closer who closed it.

videos.title: Davis' game-tying two-run homer
videos.description: Rajai Davis hits a two-run homer off Aroldis Chapman in the eighth inning of Game 7, tying the World Series at 6.

damage.stakes: Game 7, eighth inning, a three-run lead. The homer tied it.

title: Smoltz for Alexander
summary: On August 12, 1987, Detroit sent a 20-year-old in Double-A to Atlanta for Doyle Alexander. Alexander went 9–0 down the stretch. The prospect was John Smoltz.
story:
August 12, 1987. The Tigers trail Toronto by a game and a half and want a pitcher they already know.

They get Doyle Alexander, 36, who is 5–10 with a 4.13 earned-run average for the Braves. In return Atlanta takes John Smoltz, a 22nd-round pick two years earlier, then 4–10 with a 5.68 earned-run average at Double-A Glens Falls. General manager Bill Lajoie says the obvious thing: Alexander is a proven starter, and the rotation needs to be stronger. The club's other choice, in the account of the negotiations, was Steve Searcy, who was closer to the majors. Detroit kept him.

Alexander makes 11 starts and goes 9–0 with a 1.53 earned-run average. Detroit wins the American League East and loses the Championship Series to the Twins in five games. He is an All-Star in 1988 and is out of baseball after 1989.

Smoltz reaches Atlanta in 1988. He wins a Cy Young Award, saves 154 games after Tommy John surgery moved him to the bullpen, and is the only pitcher with 200 wins and 150 saves. He goes into the Hall of Fame in 2015.

The trade did what Detroit asked of it in 1987. The retelling collapses that into a theft, which skips the pennant race Lajoie was actually in. What it does not skip is the scale of the arm the Braves' scout, John Hagemann, had talked Bobby Cox into taking.
counterfactual: Detroit keeps the 20-year-old, or sends Searcy instead. Alexander pitches for someone else that August. The Tigers may not win the East in 1987. They also do not watch 200 wins and 150 saves accumulate in Atlanta. Hagemann's report stays in a file, and the Hall of Fame speech, if it still happens, happens somewhere else.

images.caption: John Smoltz at Dobbins Air Reserve Base on April 6, 2007, twenty years after Detroit traded him. This is not the day of the deal.
images.credit: U.S. Air Force photo by Don Peek, public domain.

damage.stakes: A game and a half out in August. A 20-year-old in Double-A for a pitcher the club wanted that month.

title: Johnson for Langston
summary: Seattle could not sign Mark Langston and sent him to Montreal for three pitchers. One of them was Randy Johnson, 25 years old and 6-foot-10.
story:
May 25, 1989. The Mariners have just lost at Fenway Park, 10–0, and Mark Langston has turned down a three-year, $7.1 million contract the same day. He can be a free agent after the season.

Seattle sends him, and a player to be named later, to the Expos for Randy Johnson, Brian Holman, and Gene Harris. On July 31 the player to be named is Mike Campbell. Woody Woodward, running baseball operations in Seattle, says the club has looked at a lot of packages and had to get pitching.

Johnson had been a second-round pick in 1985 and had reached Montreal in 1988. He is 25, and already the tallest pitcher the game has had, at 6-foot-10. He has not settled into a rotation. Langston is the pitcher a contender can use that summer. Dave Dombrowski, then with the Expos, says the deal gives Montreal a quality left-hander to put with Dennis Martínez, Kevin Gross, and Bryn Smith.

Langston does pitch well in Montreal and leaves as a free agent. Johnson stays in Seattle and becomes one of the great left-handers of the next two decades. The day of the trade, the surprise in the papers is that a signed ace has been exchanged for three pitchers who have not yet proved they are major-league starters. The name that mattered was not yet the name on the back of the card.

images.caption: Randy Johnson with the Yankees in 2006. The photograph is not the May 25, 1989 trade.
images.credit: Googie man, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

title: Cabrera to Detroit
summary: At the 2007 winter meetings the Marlins sent Miguel Cabrera and Dontrelle Willis to Detroit for six players, headed by Cameron Maybin and Andrew Miller.
story:
December 4, 2007. The winter meetings in Nashville.

The Florida Marlins trade Miguel Cabrera and Dontrelle Willis to the Tigers for Cameron Maybin, Andrew Miller, Mike Rabelo, Burke Badenhop, Dallas Trahern, and Eulogio De La Cruz. Maybin and Miller are the prospects the deal is built on. Cabrera is 24 and already one of the league's best hitters. Willis is the other All-Star in the package, and the reason it is not a one-player sale.

Detroit is adding him to a lineup that already has Magglio Ordóñez, Gary Sheffield, Carlos Guillén, and Iván Rodríguez. The cost is public the day it is made: two of the organization's best young players, plus four more. That is the part the shorthand drops when the trade is remembered as Cabrera for a pile of names that did not become stars.

In 2012 Cabrera wins the American League Triple Crown in a Tigers uniform. Willis does not become the pitcher the package had advertised. Maybin and Miller have major-league careers that were not the ones the prospect lists had sketched. The record of the trade is both things at once: a steep price, paid, and a hitter who was not finished.

images.caption: Miguel Cabrera with the Tigers on May 9, 2008. The photograph is the season after the trade, not the day of the deal.
images.credit: kw111786, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

videos.title: Cabrera changed the Tigers' course
videos.description: Tigers reporter Jason Beck looks back on the 2007 winter-meetings trade for Miguel Cabrera.

title: Alvarez for Fields
summary: On the 2016 trade deadline the Dodgers sent Yordan Alvarez, 19 and still without a professional game in the United States, to Houston for reliever Josh Fields.
story:
August 1, 2016. The deadline.

The Dodgers acquire Josh Fields from the Astros for Yordan Alvarez. Fields is 30. He has a 6.89 earned-run average in 15 appearances for Houston that year and a 1.65 earned-run average in 23 games at Triple-A Fresno. Alvarez is 19. The Dodgers signed him out of Cuba on June 15. He has not yet played a professional game in their system. The Dodgers' announcement describes him as a minor-league first baseman and Fields as the reliever they are adding.

Houston's general manager, Jeff Luhnow, spends that deadline saying the club will not trade Alex Bregman, Joe Musgrove, or A.J. Reed. Alvarez is not on that list. He is a teenager the Dodgers have owned for six weeks. Fields is a major-league arm in a pennant race. That was the exchange as it was written on the day.

Alvarez reached Houston in 2019 and became a middle-of-the-order hitter. Fields's time with the Dodgers did not change the way the deadline is remembered. The entry is the gap between a reliever a contender could use in August and a player who had not yet taken the field.

images.caption: Yordan Alvarez batting for Houston on September 21, 2019, his first major-league season. This is not the August 1, 2016 trade, which came before he had played in the United States.

title: Tatis for Shields
summary: The White Sox sent Fernando Tatis Jr., 17 and still without a professional game, and Erik Johnson to San Diego for James Shields and a large share of his contract.
story:
June 4, 2016. The Padres trade James Shields and cash to the White Sox for Erik Johnson and Fernando Tatis Jr.

Shields is 34, in the second season of a four-year, $75 million contract, and is 2–7 with a 4.28 earned-run average. His previous start, in Seattle, was ten earned runs in two and two-thirds innings. About $58 million remains on the deal. San Diego keeps more than half of it. Chicago's share, if Shields does not opt out, is $5 million that year and $22 million after.

Johnson is 26 and has already started in the majors. Tatis is 17, signed by Chicago the previous July, and has not made his professional debut. He is the son of a major leaguer. He is not, that afternoon, the player the trade is explained as. Preller said it was hard to move Shields and that the return was two players the Padres were excited about, plus flexibility.

The flexibility was the money. The excitement, in the retelling, is entirely the 17-year-old. Both were in the announcement. Only one of them is why the trade is filed here.

title: Betts to the Dodgers
summary: Boston sent Mookie Betts and David Price to Los Angeles for Alex Verdugo, Jeter Downs, and Connor Wong. A three-team version of the deal had already collapsed over a medical file.
story:
February 10, 2020. The Red Sox trade Mookie Betts, David Price, and cash to the Dodgers for Alex Verdugo, Jeter Downs, and Connor Wong.

Betts is the 2018 Most Valuable Player, 27 years old, and a year from free agency. The Dodgers are taking his $27 million salary for 2020. The clubs split the $96 million still owed to Price; Boston sends $48 million of it. A three-team structure with the Twins had been reported the week before, with Brusdar Graterol headed to Boston. The Red Sox backed away after reviewing his medical records. Graterol went to Los Angeles instead, in a separate trade that sent Kenta Maeda to Minnesota.

Chaim Bloom said the aim was a roster that could keep winning, and that Verdugo, Downs, and Wong put the club in a better position to do that. The competitive-balance tax was the other stated pressure: a third straight season over the threshold carried penalties Boston was trying to get out from under. Verdugo was a major-league outfielder. Downs and Wong were prospects.

Betts stayed in Los Angeles and was a central player on a championship club that autumn. The trade is not only the tax bill, and it is not only the trophy. It is a franchise batting title-winner, one season short of the open market, moved with a large contract attached so the prospect return would be smaller than his name.

title: Bautista for Diaz
summary: On August 21, 2008, Pittsburgh sent Jose Bautista to Toronto on waivers for a player to be named. Four days later the player was catcher Robinzon Diaz.
story:
August 21, 2008. A waiver claim.

Jose Bautista is in his fourth season with the Pirates and has already been a Pirate, an Oriole, a Royal, and a Devil Ray. In 2008 he hit .242 with 12 home runs and 44 runs batted in over 107 games, then lost the third-base job when Andy LaRoche arrived and was sent to Indianapolis. No National League club claimed him on trade waivers. Toronto did.

The Blue Jays acquire him for a player to be named later. On August 25 that player is Robinzon Diaz, a 24-year-old catcher in the minors.

J.P. Ricciardi, the Toronto general manager, said later that the club had ranked Diaz a C prospect and that a C prospect for a major-league player had looked like a simple exchange. Pittsburgh had asked first about another catcher, Brian Jeroloman, and Toronto had said no. Scott Rolen was hurt, and the Blue Jays wanted someone who could play third and then move. Diaz, for his part, said afterward that nobody knew the future, and that at the time he was a prospect too.

In 2010 Bautista hit 54 home runs and led the majors. The waiver trade did not predict that. It moved a bench player the Pirates had already optioned, for a catcher their trading partner was willing to spare. The home runs are what the retelling starts with. The waiver wire is what the transaction was.

title: Pierzynski Runs to First
summary: In the ninth inning of the 2005 ALCS, strike three got to Josh Paul and the Angels left the field. Doug Eddings ruled the ball had touched the ground. A.J. Pierzynski ran to first.
story:
October 12, 2005. U.S. Cellular Field, Game 2 of the American League Championship Series.

The score is tied, 1–1, in the ninth, with two out and nobody on. Mark Buehrle has pitched the whole game for Chicago. A.J. Pierzynski swings through a full-count split-finger from Kelvim Escobar. Home-plate umpire Doug Eddings closes his fist, the signal for a strike. Catcher Josh Paul — in the game because José Molina was lifted for a pinch-runner in the eighth — rolls the ball toward the mound. Escobar starts off the field.

Pierzynski takes a step toward the dugout and then runs to first. Eddings lets him stay. The umpire's account is that the fist meant strike three, not an out, because the ball had hit the ground before it reached the glove. An uncaught third strike is a live ball. Paul and the Angels had treated the inning as over.

Pablo Ozuna pinch-runs, steals second, and Joe Crede doubles him home. The White Sox win, 2–1.

One camera angle looks like a catch. Another looks like the ball touched dirt. Ken Williams, the White Sox general manager, said Paul dropped it. The Angels said he did not. Eddings did not change the call. The series, tied at a game apiece, went to Anaheim, and Chicago won the next three.

The play is filed as a ruling, not as a punch line: the rule is real, the signal was incomplete, and the runner took the base the rule gave him if the ball was on the ground.
counterfactual: Eddings's fist means the inning is over, or Paul is ruled to have caught it. Pierzynski walks to the dugout. Extra innings, maybe. Crede never doubles home Ozuna. The series still might have gone to Chicago. It would not have turned on a split-finger that one camera said was caught.

title: Knoblauch Stays on the Bag
summary: In the twelfth inning of the 1998 ALCS, a throw hit Travis Fryman and rolled away. Chuck Knoblauch stayed at first base to argue. Enrique Wilson scored from first.
story:
October 7, 1998. Yankee Stadium, Game 2.

The Championship Series is tied at a game apiece only after this one: the Indians had lost the opener, and the score here is 1–1 after eleven innings. In the twelfth Jim Thome singles. Travis Fryman bunts down the first-base line. Tino Martinez fields it and throws to Chuck Knoblauch, covering first. The ball hits Fryman, who is running inside the line, in the back, and rolls toward the right-field grass.

The umpires do not call interference. Knoblauch stays on the bag and points, waiting for the out. Enrique Wilson, pinch-running for Thome, keeps going and scores from first, stumbling as he gets close to the plate. Kenny Lofton follows with a two-run single. Cleveland wins, 4–1.

Knoblauch said afterward that his foot was on the base, that he expected the call, and that arguing was an instantaneous reaction.

The interference the Yankees wanted was a judgment the crew did not make. The ball was still in play while that argument happened. Wilson's run is the part that does not depend on the call. A live ball went past the fielder whose job, once the throw missed, was to pick it up.

title: Gossage Pitches to Gibson
summary: In the eighth inning of the 1984 World Series, Dick Williams wanted Goose Gossage to walk Kirk Gibson. Gossage talked him out of it. Gibson hit a three-run homer.
story:
October 14, 1984. Tiger Stadium, Game 5.

Detroit leads the Series three games to one and the game, 5–4, in the bottom of the eighth. Lance Parrish has homered off Rich Gossage in the seventh. Kurt Bevacqua has homered off Willie Hernández in the eighth to bring San Diego within a run. Marty Castillo and Lou Whitaker are on base when Kirk Gibson comes up, and first base is open. The next hitter is Parrish.

Dick Williams comes to the mound. The account from the dugout, and from Gibson, is that Williams wanted the intentional walk — a left-handed hitter put on so Gossage could face the right-handed Parrish. Gossage talks him out of it.

Sparky Anderson holds up four fingers in the Detroit dugout. Gibson said he held up ten fingers and bet Anderson ten dollars he would hit it out. He hits a three-run homer into the right-field stands. The Tigers lead, 8–4, and win the Series when Hernández finishes the ninth.

Williams changed his mind on the mound, in public, at the urging of his closer. That is a managerial decision with a name on it, the same shape as pitching to a dangerous hitter with a base open. Gibson earned the swing. The entry is the conversation that let him have it.

title: Three Errors by Conrad
summary: In Game 3 of the 2010 NLDS, Brooks Conrad made three errors. The last one, on a two-out grounder in the ninth, let the Giants take a lead they did not give back.
story:
October 10, 2010. Turner Field, Game 3, attendance 53,284.

The Braves and Giants have split the first two games, each of them decided by a run. Brooks Conrad is at second base because Chipper Jones and Martín Prado are out for the season. He is 30, a journeyman, and he has already been charged with errors late in the regular season. In this game he bobbles a grounder in the first, and that one does not score. In the second he drops a popup, and an unearned run does.

The Braves lead, 2–1, into the ninth on Eric Hinske's homer. With two out, San Francisco ties the game against Craig Kimbrel. Buster Posey then hits a grounder that goes under Conrad's glove. Freddy Sánchez scores. The Giants lead, 3–2. Brian Wilson finishes the ninth. Kimbrel is the losing pitcher.

Conrad has three errors, tying a postseason record for a game, and he said afterward that it was completely embarrassing.

The series was not over. San Francisco won Game 4 the next night and the Division Series in four. The three errors are still the picture of Game 3, and the ninth is the one that changed the score. The first of them did not. A record of three is not the same fact as three runs.

title: Hudson and the Immaculate Inning
summary: Yoshinobu Yamamoto was one called strike from an immaculate inning when Marvin Hudson ruled a 96-mph fastball a ball. Yamamoto struck out the side anyway. The inning was no longer immaculate.
story:
June 19, 2025. Dodger Stadium, the Padres in town.

In the top of the third Yoshinobu Yamamoto strikes out Bryce Johnson and Martín Maldonado on three pitches each. He gets ahead of Fernando Tatis Jr., 0–2. The next pitch is a 96-mph fastball over the middle of the plate. Plate umpire Marvin Hudson calls it a ball.

An immaculate inning is three strikeouts on nine pitches. There have been about 118 of them in major-league history. Hudson's call ends this one. Yamamoto strikes Tatis out two pitches later, so the side is still retired on strikes, and the pitch count is no longer nine. San Diego wins the game, 5–3. Accounts in the East often date the night June 20. In Los Angeles it was still the 19th.

Dodgers broadcaster Joe Davis asked on the air whether the league could borrow the automated ball-strike system from Triple-A for the night. The entry is the one pitch. The strikeout that followed does not put the call back.

title: Cash Pulls Snell
summary: Blake Snell led Game 6 of the World Series on 73 pitches when Kevin Cash took him out after a one-out single. Nick Anderson allowed the tying and go-ahead runs. The Dodgers won the championship.
story:
October 27, 2020. Globe Life Field in Arlington, Game 6.

The Rays lead, 1–0, in the sixth. Blake Snell has thrown 73 pitches, struck out nine, and allowed two hits. With one out, Austin Barnes singles.

Kevin Cash comes and gets him.

Nick Anderson relieves. The tying run scores, and then the go-ahead run. Los Angeles wins, 3–1, and wins the series. Snell had been the best pitcher on the field. The inning he left became the inning the season ended.

Cash's account was that the matchups, and a third time through a lineup that had already seen Snell, were the reason. Snell said afterward that he had wanted to stay. The entry keeps both sentences. A decision can be the one the model recommended and still be the one the game punished.
counterfactual: Cash leaves him in. Barnes is on first with one out, and Snell — nine strikeouts, two hits, 73 pitches — faces the next man. He might have gotten through the sixth. He might not have. What does not happen is Anderson inheriting the inning that ends the season. The 1–0 lead gets a longer look.

title: Phillips, Taylor, and the Relay
summary: With two outs in the ninth of World Series Game 4, Brett Phillips singled, Chris Taylor bobbled the ball, and the relay home never got there. Randy Arozarena tripped on the way and still scored.
story:
October 24, 2020. Globe Life Field, Game 4.

The Dodgers are one strike from a 7–6 win and a lead of three games to one. Brett Phillips, with two outs, singles to center. Chris Taylor, the center fielder, does not field the ball cleanly. The relay comes home. Catcher Will Smith does not catch it. Kenley Jansen, the pitcher, is not behind the plate to back the throw up.

Randy Arozarena is the runner who has to score from first, and he goes down rounding third. He gets up and comes home anyway. Tampa Bay wins, 8–7. The series is tied. Los Angeles wins it two nights later.

The single was a hit. The rest was a sequence of ordinary baseball jobs, each of them missed in order: the pickup, the throw, the catch, the backup. Arozarena's fall is the picture people remember. The run scored because the ball was still loose when he arrived.

title: Three Calls, Four Innings
summary: In the first four innings of a 2018 division-series game, first-base umpire Ángel Hernández had three calls overturned by replay. Two involved Didi Gregorius. One involved Gleyber Torres.
story:
October 8, 2018. Yankee Stadium, Game 3 of the American League Division Series.

Ángel Hernández is at first base. In the first four innings, replay overturns him three times. Two of the plays are on Didi Gregorius. The third is on Gleyber Torres. Boston wins the game, 16–1. The score makes the calls irrelevant to the result and impossible to miss on the broadcast.

Hernández already had a reputation, including a racial-discrimination lawsuit against Major League Baseball that did not succeed. This night became the short version of that reputation: three reversals before the fifth inning of a playoff game. He retired on May 27, 2024.

A reversed call is the system working. Three of them in four innings is the entry. The lawsuit is context for why the night was received as it was.

title: The Yankees' Fifth Inning
summary: The Yankees led Game 5 of the World Series by five runs. Aaron Judge dropped a fly ball, Anthony Volpe bounced a throw, and Gerrit Cole did not cover first. The Dodgers scored five unearned runs and won the championship.
story:
October 30, 2024. Yankee Stadium, Game 5.

New York leads, 5–0. In the fifth, Tommy Edman hits a routine fly to center. Aaron Judge drops it. Anthony Volpe, the shortstop, then bounces a throw to third. Gerrit Cole, the pitcher, does not cover first on a ground ball by Mookie Betts.

The Dodgers score five unearned runs and tie the game. They win it, 7–6, and win the series. Freddie Freeman had already been the story of the series at the plate. This inning was the field.

None of the three mistakes was exotic. A fly ball, a throw, a pitcher covering a base. Filed together they are the inning a five-run lead left. Separately, each one is a play a major-league club makes, and misses, in April.
counterfactual: Judge squeezes it. Volpe's throw is clean. Cole covers first. Three ordinary plays, and the fifth inning stays a 5–0 game. Los Angeles still has Freeman. New York still has to finish a World Series. The lead does not leave on errors.

title: The Ball in Betts's Glove
summary: Mookie Betts caught Gleyber Torres's foul against the right-field wall. Two fans grabbed his glove and tried to take the ball. Torres was called out for interference, and the fans were barred from the next game.
story:
October 29, 2024. Yankee Stadium, Game 4 of the World Series, the bottom of the first.

Gleyber Torres hits a foul fly toward the right-field seats. Mookie Betts reaches the wall and catches it. Two fans in the front row take hold of his glove and his wrist and try to pull the ball out.

The umpires rule fan interference. Torres is out. The two fans are ejected, and they are banned from Game 5. The catch counts. The argument is about whose hands had been on the glove.

A fan reaching over a wall is an old entry in this catalog. This one is on film from a yard away, in a World Series, with the ball already in the glove. The ruling followed the rule. The entry is the reach.

title: Britton Stays in the Bullpen
summary: Buck Showalter saved Zach Britton, who had converted all 47 of his saves with a 0.54 earned-run average, for a lead that never came. Ubaldo Jiménez gave up a three-run walk-off homer in the eleventh.
story:
October 4, 2016. Rogers Centre, the American League Wild Card Game.

The game is tied into the eleventh. Zach Britton has been the best reliever in the league that year: a 0.54 earned-run average, and 47 saves in 47 chances. Buck Showalter does not bring him in. He is waiting for a lead to protect.

Ubaldo Jiménez, a starter having a poor season, pitches the eleventh. Edwin Encarnación hits a three-run homer. Toronto wins, 5–2, and Baltimore's season ends with Britton still in the bullpen.

There had not been a save situation. There had been an elimination inning.

The decision has a logic if a closer is defined as a man who pitches only with a lead. The game did not offer that inning. It offered a tie, in October, with the club's best pitcher available. Showalter kept the definition and lost the game.
counterfactual: Showalter calls for Britton. The best reliever in the league that year faces Encarnación in a tie, in October. He might still have given up the homer. He might have ended the inning. Baltimore's season would not have ended with him standing in the bullpen, unused.

title: Harvey Talks His Way Back
summary: Terry Collins let Matt Harvey pitch the ninth of World Series Game 5 with a two-run lead. Harvey walked a man and gave up a double. Eric Hosmer then scored the tying run on a throw Lucas Duda did not get to the plate.
story:
November 1, 2015. Citi Field, Game 5.

The Mets lead, 2–0, in the ninth. Terry Collins had planned to bring in Jeurys Familia. Matt Harvey, who has pitched eight innings, asks to go back out, and Collins lets him. Harvey walks Lorenzo Cain and gives up an RBI double to Eric Hosmer. The lead is one.

Salvador Pérez then hits a ground ball. Hosmer breaks for home. Lucas Duda's throw from first is wide of the plate, and Hosmer scores the tying run. Kansas City wins, 7–2, in the twelfth, and wins the series.

Two decisions are in the inning. Collins changed his mind on the mound, in public, at the request of his starter. Hosmer, seeing the ball on the ground, ran. Duda's throw is the play that made the run. The conversation is why Harvey was still the pitcher when the inning began.

title: Girardi Does Not Challenge
summary: A two-out pitch was ruled to have hit Lonnie Chisenhall. Replays showed it had hit the bat. Joe Girardi did not challenge. Francisco Lindor then hit a grand slam.
story:
October 6, 2017. Progressive Field, Game 2 of the American League Division Series.

With two out, a pitch is ruled to have hit Lonnie Chisenhall. The replay shows it coming off the knob of the bat and into the catcher's glove, which would have been strike three and the end of the inning. Joe Girardi has a challenge. He does not use it.

Francisco Lindor hits a grand slam. Cleveland wins, 9–8, in thirteen innings. Girardi said afterward that he regretted the decision. New York still won the series.

The rule gave the manager a look. He declined it. The slam is what the inning became after that. The entry is the choice not to ask, made with the picture already on the scoreboard.

title: Kershaw, Then Kelly
summary: Dave Roberts brought Clayton Kershaw in to protect a two-run lead, and Anthony Rendon and Juan Soto homered back to back. Joe Kelly then pitched a second inning, and Howie Kendrick hit a grand slam.
story:
October 9, 2019. Dodger Stadium, Game 5 of the National League Division Series.

Los Angeles has won 106 games. The Dodgers lead, 3–1, in the eighth when Dave Roberts brings Clayton Kershaw out of the bullpen. Anthony Rendon homers. Juan Soto homers. The game is tied.

In the tenth Roberts sends Joe Kelly back out for a second inning of relief. Howie Kendrick hits a grand slam. Washington wins, 7–3, and goes on to win the World Series. The Dodgers' season ends at home, in a winner-take-all game, on two pitching decisions.

Kershaw had been the club's best starter for a decade. Using him there was a choice about the eighth inning of a series, not a statement about his career. Kelly's second inning is the other choice. Kendrick's swing is what the second one cost.

title: Turner in the Runner's Lane
summary: In World Series Game 6, Trea Turner was called out for runner's-lane interference on a bunt, and a run came off the board. The rule's wording became the argument. Washington won the series anyway.
story:
October 29, 2019. Minute Maid Park, Game 6, the top of the seventh.

Trea Turner bunts and runs to first. He and Yuli Gurriel, the first baseman, meet at the bag. Home-plate umpire Sam Holbrook calls Turner out for interfering while running outside the runner's lane. A run that had scored on the play is taken off the board.

Dave Martinez, the Washington manager, is ejected in the argument. The rule requires the runner to be in the lane when a throw is being made to first, and it is written more narrowly than the play looks on a broadcast. Washington wins the game, 7–2, and wins the series the next night.

The call followed a sentence in the book. The sentence is why the play is filed here, with the pine-tar game and the infield fly: a rule applied in October, in front of a country that had not read it, and a run removed because of where a runner's feet were.

title: The Check Swing
summary: With the tying run on base in the ninth of a winner-take-all game, Wilmer Flores held up on an 0–2 slider. First-base umpire Gabe Morales ruled that he had swung. The Giants' season ended.
story:
October 14, 2021. Oracle Park, Game 5 of the National League Division Series.

San Francisco has won 107 games. In the ninth, with the tying run on, Wilmer Flores takes an 0–2 slider from Max Scherzer and appears to stop his swing. Gabe Morales, umpiring at first, rules that he has gone.

It is strike three. The series is over.

A check swing is one of the few calls replay does not review. The batter, the catcher, and the first-base umpire share a judgment the broadcast then tries to settle with a freeze frame. Morales's judgment ended a postseason series. It was the first time one had ended on a check-swing strikeout.

The Giants' season was 107 wins and this pitch. The entry is not that they lost a series. It is that the last out was a question the rulebook leaves to one man's eyes, and that those eyes said swing.
counterfactual: Morales says he held up. The at-bat goes on. Flores still has to beat Scherzer. The Giants still have to score the tying run. A winner-take-all game is not decided by a check swing — because the umpire saw it the other way. The 107-win season gets at least one more pitch.

title: Craig Chases Báez
summary: A throw pulled Will Craig off first base with two outs. Instead of getting back to the bag, he chased Javier Báez toward home. Willson Contreras scored from second, and Báez ended up on second base.
story:
May 27, 2021. PNC Park, the Cubs in Pittsburgh.

With two outs, Javier Báez hits a routine ground ball. The throw pulls first baseman Will Craig off the bag. The out is still available if Craig steps back on the base. He runs after Báez instead.

Báez retreats toward home. Willson Contreras, the runner on second, comes around and scores. Throws after that put Báez on second. Chicago wins, 5–3. The next day Craig called it baseball 101.

The play is a rundown run backward. The first baseman left the base he was supposed to keep, the batter ran the wrong direction on purpose, and a run scored on a ball that had been an out. Craig's sentence the next day is the right size for it. The catalog does not need a larger one.

title: Miller for Swanson
summary: Six months after drafting Dansby Swanson first overall, Arizona traded him, Ender Inciarte, and Aaron Blair to Atlanta for Shelby Miller. Miller went 3–12 with a 6.15 earned-run average the next year.
story:
December 9, 2015. The Diamondbacks trade Dansby Swanson, Ender Inciarte, and Aaron Blair to the Braves for Shelby Miller.

Swanson is the first pick in the draft that June. Inciarte is a center fielder already playing a Gold Glove defense. Blair is a pitching prospect. Miller is a major-league starter Arizona believes it can win with immediately.

In 2016 Miller goes 3–12 with a 6.15 earned-run average and is sent to the minors. Swanson becomes Atlanta's shortstop and wins a World Series there in 2021.

The trade did not fail because the prospects were famous on the day it was made. Swanson had not played in the majors. It failed because the pitcher, who was the known quantity, was not the pitcher the deal required.

A deadline trade of a star for prospects is one shape. This is the other: three players, one of them the first pick in the country, for one year of a starter who then lost twelve games.

images.caption: Shelby Miller at 2016 spring training, shortly after the trade. Not a photo of the trade.

title: Archer to Pittsburgh
summary: At the 2018 deadline Pittsburgh sent Tyler Glasnow, Austin Meadows, and Shane Baz to Tampa Bay for Chris Archer. Archer's earned-run average in Pittsburgh stayed over 5. Meadows and Glasnow became the players the prospects had been advertised as.
story:
July 31, 2018. The deadline.

The Pirates trade Tyler Glasnow, Austin Meadows, and a player to be named later to the Rays for Chris Archer. The player named later is Shane Baz. Archer is the established starter, a former All-Star, and the pitcher a club adds when it thinks the race is still open.

His earned-run average in Pittsburgh stays above 5. He misses 2020 after thoracic-outlet surgery, and the club declines his option. Meadows is an All-Star in 2019. Glasnow becomes the Rays' ace. Baz was still a prospect on the day of the deal. He was also the third name.

The trade is the deadline version of an old entry: a pitcher whose present was bought with someone else's future, and a present that did not arrive. Archer's injury is part of the record. It is not the whole of why the return outgrew him.

images.caption: Chris Archer with the Pirates, August 2018, right after the trade. Not a photo of the trade.

title: Arozarena to Tampa
summary: St. Louis traded Randy Arozarena and José Martínez for Matthew Liberatore and other pieces. That October Arozarena hit ten home runs in the postseason, a record, on the way to the World Series.
story:
January 9, 2020. The Cardinals trade Randy Arozarena and José Martínez to the Rays. The pitching prospect coming back is Matthew Liberatore, with other pieces in the deal.

Arozarena is an outfielder who reached the majors the year before and has not yet had a season of his own.

Ten months later he hits ten home runs in one postseason, a record, during Tampa Bay's run to the World Series. In 2021 he is the American League Rookie of the Year. He is an All-Star after that. Liberatore's career is not the career the ten home runs made the trade look like on a replay.

The entry is the gap between a January transaction and an October record. Arozarena was not that hitter on the day St. Louis moved him. He was that hitter before the year was over.

title: Davis Goes 0-for-54
summary: In the middle of a seven-year, $161 million contract, Chris Davis went 0-for-54, the longest hitless streak by a position player in major-league history. The streak ended on April 13, 2019.
story:
April 13, 2019. The streak ends. What it leaves behind is a number.

It ran from September 15, 2018, to this date. Fifty-four at-bats without a hit is the longest hitless run by a position player in major-league history. Chris Davis is in the third and fourth years of a seven-year, $161 million contract, at the time the largest in Orioles history. He hit .168 in 2018.

He retired with money from the deal still owed, much of it deferred. The at-bats are a hitting record. The contract is why the record is also a front-office entry. Baltimore paid for the hitter Davis had been, across a stretch in which he stopped getting hits at all.

A slump is ordinary. Fifty-four is the length that makes it a record. The entry keeps the number and the deal in the same sentence, because neither one, alone, is why it is filed here.

images.caption: Chris Davis in the Orioles dugout, April 10, 2019, during the hitless streak (it ended April 13). Not a specific at-bat.
images.credit: Keith Allison: Flickr, e-mail, Twitter, Instagram, website / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0)

title: Scherzer's Hand
summary: In the fourth inning at Dodger Stadium, the umpires checked Max Scherzer's hand and glove, ruled them too sticky, and threw him out. Major League Baseball suspended him ten games. He said it was rosin and sweat.
story:
April 19, 2023. Dodger Stadium, the Mets in town.

In the fourth inning the umpires, Phil Cuzzi and Dan Bellino among them, inspect Max Scherzer under the foreign-substance rules the league has been enforcing since 2021. They judge his hand and his glove too sticky and eject him.

Scherzer says it is rosin and sweat. The league suspends him ten games. The rule was written because pitchers had been using substances that were not rosin, and the spin rates had shown it. A check in the middle of an inning is the enforcement. An ejection is the judgment that this hand had crossed the line.

The entry is that judgment, and Scherzer's answer to it. The ten games are what the league added after the night was over.

title: A Game Ends on the Clock
summary: On the first full day of the pitch clock, Cal Conley was not set in the box at the eight-second mark with the bases loaded in the ninth. Umpire John Libka called an automatic strike three, and a spring game ended in a tie.
story:
February 25, 2023. A spring-training game in North Port, Florida, Braves against Red Sox.

It is the first full day of the new pitch clock. The bases are loaded in the bottom of the ninth, the count is full, and there are two outs. Cal Conley, the batter, is not in the box and set when the eight-second clock runs out.

John Libka calls strike three. The game ends, 6–6.

Robert Kwiatkowski is the pitcher. The clock records the last out before he has to throw another pitch. Spring training is where a rule is supposed to look strange before it looks ordinary, and this one announced itself by ending a game.

The entry is that ending: the first time a clock, rather than a swing or a call of the eye, recorded the last out of a major-league exhibition.

title: Mizuhara's Debts
summary: During the Seoul Series, the Dodgers fired Ippei Mizuhara, Shohei Ohtani's interpreter. Mizuhara had stolen about $17 million from Ohtani's account to pay illegal gambling debts. He pleaded guilty. Prosecutors cleared Ohtani.
story:
March 20, 2024. The season-opening series in Seoul.

The Dodgers fire Ippei Mizuhara, who has been Shohei Ohtani's interpreter for years. What comes out in the days around the firing is that Mizuhara has taken roughly $17 million from Ohtani's bank account to cover debts from illegal sports betting.

He pleaded guilty on June 4, 2024, to bank fraud and filing a false tax return. On February 6, 2025, he was sentenced to 57 months in federal prison. Federal prosecutors said Ohtani had not been involved. For about a week the bets were treated as a question about Ohtani. The charging documents and the plea put them on Mizuhara.

The entry is the theft and the gambling that the theft was for. The catalog's subject is the person who had the debts, the access, and the guilty plea.

title: Marcano's Lifetime Ban
summary: Major League Baseball banned Tucupita Marcano for life for betting on baseball, including 25 bets on Pirates games while he was on Pittsburgh's roster. It was the first lifetime gambling ban since Pete Rose in 1989.
story:
June 4, 2024. Major League Baseball bans Tucupita Marcano for life.

He had bet on baseball. Twenty-five of the bets were on Pittsburgh games while he was on the Pirates' roster, on the injured list. He was with the Padres by the time the ban was announced. Four other players were suspended for one year. Marcano was the one who did not get a return date.

A lifetime ban for gambling on the game had not been issued since Pete Rose in 1989. The rule is older than either of them. A player does not bet on baseball, and he does not bet on his own club. Marcano had done both, from the injured list, which is still the roster.

The entry records the ban and the number of bets. It does not need the comparison to do the work. The comparison is why the date is in the catalog at all.

title: Clase and Ortiz Are Indicted
summary: Federal prosecutors charged Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz with rigging pitches for bettors. The indictment alleges the bettors won at least $450,000. Both pitchers had already been placed on leave. The case was not finished when the charges were made public.
story:
November 9, 2025. The indictment, returned four days earlier in federal court in Brooklyn, is unsealed.

Prosecutors charge Cleveland pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz with agreeing, in advance, to the speed and type of particular pitches so that bettors could wager on them. The indictment alleges that the arrangement with Clase went back to 2023, that the pitches often went in the dirt, and that Ortiz joined in June 2025. It alleges the bettors won at least $450,000.

Ortiz had been placed on leave on July 3, 2025. Both pitchers were on leave through the summer. A superseding indictment was filed on February 12, 2026. An indictment is a set of charges. It is not a verdict. This entry states the charges and the leave. It does not state a result the court had not reached.

What the catalog can file, on the date the charges were unsealed, is that two major-league pitchers were accused of selling the shape of a pitch. The pitches named in the indictment were not alleged to have decided a pennant. They were alleged to have been decided before they were thrown.

images.caption: Emmanuel Clase pitching for the Guardians at Progressive Field, May 14, 2023. Not related to the indictment.

title: Hoberg Is Fired
summary: Pat Hoberg, one of the league's most accurate ball-strike umpires, was fired for sharing legal betting accounts with a poker player who bet on baseball, and for deleting messages. Major League Baseball found no evidence he had bet on the game himself.
story:
May 31, 2024. The firing takes effect.

Pat Hoberg had called a perfect plate game in the 2022 World Series and was, by the league's own tracking, among the most accurate ball-strike umpires working. He is dismissed for sharing legal sports-betting accounts with a professional poker player who bet on baseball, and for deleting messages that mattered to the investigation.

Major League Baseball said it found no evidence that Hoberg had bet on baseball or changed the outcome of a game. His appeal was denied on February 3, 2025. The finding and the firing are both part of the record. Accuracy behind the plate did not answer the question the league was asking, which was about the accounts and the deleted messages.

The entry is an umpire punished for the company of a bet, not for a call. The calls, including a perfect World Series plate, are why the punishment was news. They are not what he was fired for.

title: The Throw That Hit the Bat
summary: Russell Martin's throw back to the pitcher hit Shin-Soo Choo's bat. The ball was live, Rougned Odor scored from third, and the Rogers Centre threw trash.
story:
October 14, 2015. Rogers Centre, Game 5 of the American League Division Series, the top of the seventh.

Russell Martin, the Toronto catcher, makes the ordinary throw back to the pitcher. The ball hits Shin-Soo Choo's bat as Choo stands in the box and rolls away. Rougned Odor scores from third. Texas leads, 3–2.

The ball is live. Dale Scott's crew lets the run stand, which is what the rule required. Fans throw bottles and trash, and the game stops. In the bottom of the inning Toronto makes three errors, and then José Bautista homers and the Blue Jays take the lead. The series ends that night.

The throw is a routine that became a run because a bat was where a bat is allowed to be. The delay is the crowd. The entry is the rule, applied once, in a game that already had a lead to lose. It is a different night from the one, a season later, when Odor and Bautista fought.

title: The Reverse Boycott
summary: On June 13, 2023, 27,759 people, the season's largest crowd, came to the Coliseum to tell John Fisher to sell the Athletics. They wore shirts that said SELL. The club left Oakland after the 2024 season.
story:
June 13, 2023. The Oakland Coliseum, the Rays in town.

The announced crowd is 27,759, the largest of the Athletics' season. The point of the night is the crowd. Fans have organized a reverse boycott of the planned move to Las Vegas: fill the park once, in shirts that read SELL, and chant for the owner to sell the team.

John Fisher is the owner the chants name. The club played its last season in Oakland in 2024 and moved its home games to Sacramento while a Las Vegas ballpark was unfinished. The protest did not stop the move. It made the argument in the building the argument was about.

A promotion fills a park by pricing beer or records. This one filled a park by asking the customers to show up and say the opposite of what the owner intended. The game was played. The entry is the reason the seats were full.

images.caption: Oakland fans protest owner John Fisher's proposed move to Las Vegas, April 28, 2023. A related protest about six weeks before the June 13 reverse boycott. Not the boycott itself.

title: The 121st Loss
summary: On September 27, 2024, the White Sox lost their 121st game and passed the 1962 Mets. They finished 41–121. The season included a franchise-record losing streak of 21.
story:
September 27, 2024. Detroit.

The White Sox lose, 4–1, and the loss is their 121st. The 1962 Mets had lost 120, which had been the modern record. Chicago finishes 41–121. During the summer the club also lost 21 in a row, a franchise record. Pedro Grifol, the manager, was fired in August. Grady Sizemore finished the season.

A hundred and twenty-one losses is not one play. It is a season that became a number, the way 120 had been a number since the Mets were new. The Mets of 1962 were an expansion club playing its first year. The White Sox of 2024 were not.

The entry is the record and the distinction. Passing an expansion team's first season, sixty-two years later, is the fact. The streak of 21 is the stretch inside it that did not need the final weekend to be obvious.

title: Bauer Throws It Over the Fence
summary: When Terry Francona came to take him out in the fifth, Trevor Bauer turned and threw the baseball over the center-field fence at Kauffman Stadium. He apologized after the game. Cleveland traded him within the week.
story:
July 28, 2019. Kauffman Stadium, the Indians in town.

In the fifth inning Terry Francona comes to the mound to remove Trevor Bauer. Bauer turns toward center field and throws the ball over the fence.

The gesture is the outing. The inning, whatever it had been, ends as a picture of a pitcher dismissing the baseball he had been paid to throw.

He apologized after the game. Within days Cleveland traded him to Cincinnati. The apology and the trade are both on the record. The ball stayed in the seats beyond the wall.

The entry is the throw. A pitcher leaving a game walks off the mound. Bauer threw the baseball out of the park.

title: Five Relievers in the Ninth
summary: Matt Moore left Game 4 of the 2016 division series with a 5–2 lead after eight innings. Bruce Bochy used five relievers in the ninth and did not use Santiago Casilla. The Cubs scored four runs, the last on Javier Báez's single.
story:
October 11, 2016. AT&T Park, Game 4 of the National League Division Series.

Matt Moore has pitched eight innings, and San Francisco leads, 5–2, going to the ninth. Bruce Bochy uses five relievers. None of them gets the inning finished cleanly. The Cubs score four runs. Javier Báez's single wins it, and Chicago wins the series.

Santiago Casilla, the closer, stays on the bench. He said afterward that he had been ready and had not been asked. A manager may have a reason to go away from his closer. Five pitchers in one inning, with a three-run lead and the series on the line, is a lot of reasons.

Moore's eight innings are the part the retelling skips. The lead was real when he left. The ninth is the entry, and Casilla's absence from it is the decision with a name.
